d: A 360-degree orbit shot circles the subject through a full turn, usually at a constant radius, always facing them. The background becomes a continuous ribbon while the person stays the center of interest.
p: Orbit clockwise 120 degrees around a violinist standing still in an empty circular hall. Keep her eyes near the same point in frame, natural live-speed motion, constant camera distance, no zoom. Columns reveal genuine changing perspective. One uninterrupted eight-second take.

d: A 3d rotation camera treats the figure as a sculptural object on a virtual turntable of space. The world may be a cyc or a void; the point is every side, not a street orbit.
p: The camera rotates in 3D around [Subject] as if on a virtual turntable.

d: An aerial shot views a large area from a high flying camera so geography reads as a map, the figure small in land or city. Helicopter, drone, or a virtual path can carry it; altitude and a stable horizon are the facts.
p: An aerial camera follows a small blue car along a winding mountain road, gradually gaining altitude as the road disappears into enormous dark forest. Smooth forward motion, stable horizon, realistic road continuity and vehicle speed, no cut.

d: An aerial pullback rises and recedes until a person or building becomes a small mark in a landscape. The move hands the scene from a character to geography, from helicopter or high-drone height rather than from a ground crane.
p: The camera rises and pulls back from [Subject] until the surrounding landscape dominates.

d: An aerial push in starts high and descends or tightens until a single figure reads in the map. It picks one human out of a city, crowd, or terrain from altitude.
p: The camera descends and pushes in from a high aerial toward [Subject].

d: An arc shot moves the camera around the subject along part of a circle while the lens stays aimed at them. A quarter or half orbit is enough: the axis of the scene changes without a cut, and the background slides.
p: The camera arcs around [Subject], always facing them, background sliding past.

d: An arc left is a curved dolly that travels partway around the subject while staying aimed at them. The camera's axis on the conversation or room changes without a cut, usually about a quarter-orbit.
p: The camera arcs left about 90 degrees around [Subject], always facing them.

d: An arc right is a partial orbit to the right, usually about a quarter turn, with the lens remaining on the subject. Background slides while eyeline and distance stay roughly constant.
p: The camera arcs right about 90 degrees around [Subject], always facing them.

d: A bolt cam hurls an ultra-high-speed camera along a crash rig toward an impact, then freezes. The punch is physical translation on a rail or pneumatic throw, not a change of focal length.
p: Ultra-fast camera strike toward [Subject], then a sudden settle, impact energy.

d: A buckle up camera straps the lens to the cabin with the subject, so the vehicle is the tripod and acceleration is the grammar. Interior stays sharp; the world streaks past the glass.
p: Camera locked in the vehicle with [Subject], the world streaking past the glass.

d: A camera roll rotates the frame around the lens axis as if the world has lost its up, either by rolling the camera or by rotating a room around a weighted body. Gravity becomes optional, which is stronger than a small Dutch cant.
p: A rigid hotel corridor slowly rolls ninety degrees while a courier braces against a wall that becomes the floor. Maintain coherent gravity, body weight, cloth motion and contact. Previsualize the room rotation in 3D, then generate short connected beats from fixed endpoints. No bending walls or effortless floating.

d: Car chase cinematography covers pursuit from a second vehicle, matching speed, the road as the set. Two machines stay in a line of action; this is the hunter's lens, not a locked interior.
p: Camera pursues [Subject] from another vehicle, matching speed, road parallax.

d: A car mount camera bolts to hood, door, or bumper so bodywork sits in the near plane and asphalt slides underneath. Chrome and road share one rigid relationship because the rig is the machine.
p: Camera mounted to the car with [Subject], bodywork in the foreground, road sliding underneath.

d: A choreographed camera times bodies and lens as one phrase of movement. The blocking is scored: steps, turns, and the support share a count, then the phrase ends.
p: Camera and [Subject] move as one choreography, a single phrase, no extra flourishes.

d: A conveyor camera treats the world as a belt: relentless lateral travel at constant speed, factory or infinite product-line geometry. The subject can stand still while the line delivers the next unit past the frame.
p: The world slides past [Subject] as if on a conveyor, constant lateral speed.

d: A crane down shot lowers the camera on an arm from a high wide view into a human-scale frame. The world collapses from map to face because the lens occupies new heights, not because it merely nods.
p: Begin high over a lively harbor market. Descend beside a woman unloading oranges, then continue at her shoulder as she walks between stalls. The high-to-ground movement feels continuous with no sudden speed or horizon change. Plan separate crane and walking sections joined at a foreground canopy if needed.

d: A crane-over lifts and arcs the camera on a jib or crane until it looks down on the scene from above. Height and angle change together in one move, turning the floor into a map.
p: The camera cranes up and over [Subject], finishing in a high downward angle.

d: A crane over the head rises on the arm until the camera looks nearly straight down, a person becoming a map. The end state is overhead, not a high three-quarter.
p: The camera cranes up and over [Subject] until the view is almost overhead.

d: A crane shot lifts the camera on a jib or Technocrane, often easing backward at the same time, so the frame climbs from a human scale into a wider view of the location. Height change is the point, and a little boom-out keeps the subject from sliding off the bottom of the frame.
p: Begin at eye level beside one volunteer carrying water. Crane upward and backward to reveal hundreds of orderly relief tents across a dry valley. One continuous shot; the volunteer becomes small but remains trackable. Realistic scale and coherent tent spacing, no sudden aerial cut.

d: A crash zoom is a rapid focal-length snap from a wider frame into a detail, usually without moving the camera. The punch is optical and conspicuous: size changes faster than a body can walk.
p: A solemn auctioneer lifts a plain wooden box. Snap-zoom instantly from a medium shot to the tiny blinking light hidden under its lid. Fixed camera position, strong punchy zoom, immediate sharp landing, no forward dolly and no slow-motion.

d: A crash zoom out is a sudden, fast widening of the lens from a tight frame into a much wider one, usually without moving the camera. It dumps the subject back into the environment in a fraction of a second.
p: Snap zoom out from [Subject] in under a second, revealing the wider scene, then hold.

d: A dolly shot places the camera on a wheeled platform so the body translates through space: doorway dolly, Fisher, Chapman. Because the nodal point moves, foreground, mid-ground, and background change in parallax, which a zoom cannot do.
p: The camera dollies, physically traveling, parallax shifting around [Subject].

d: A dolly in shot moves the entire camera through space on a wheeled or tracked support, advancing toward the subject at a measured pace. The nodal point walks, so foreground and background shift in parallax as the surroundings are progressively excluded.
p: An archivist sits at a desk and notices a familiar signature on an old letter. Begin in a medium-wide shot. Over eight seconds dolly slowly forward to a close-up, fixed lens, subtle foreground parallax, no zoom. Her eyes lift only at the end. Restrained daylight, no cut.

d: A dolly left, also called a truck left, slides the whole camera sideways to the left on wheels or track. The lens stays aimed with the subject while background planes peel past in parallax.
p: The camera slides left on a dolly, keeping [Subject] in frame, background parallax visible.

d: A dolly out shot withdraws the entire camera through space on a wheeled or tracked support. The world widens with true parallax, and the subject shrinks inside architecture because the station point has actually retreated.
p: Start tightly on a calm pianist’s face. Pull the camera backward in one uninterrupted shot, fixed focal length, gradually revealing that the grand piano stands alone in a flooded ballroom. Keep the face natural and delay the water reveal until the middle of the shot.

d: A dolly right, or truck right, moves the camera body sideways to the right without panning. New space enters from one side of the frame while the other side exits, and layered parallax proves the translation.
p: The camera slides right on a dolly, keeping [Subject] framed, smooth lateral parallax.

d: A dolly zoom combines camera movement and opposite zooming to preserve subject size while distorting perspective. It is not a zoom with a digital background stretch: translation and focal length work against each other.
p: One continuous six-second shot of a station attendant realizing a train is missing. Dolly straight backward while optically zooming in at the compensating rate. Keep her head exactly the same height and centered; the long platform behind her appears to compress. She barely moves. Stable facial identity, rigid architecture, no cut, no ordinary push-in.

d: A dolly zoom in approaches on wheels while the lens zooms out, so the figure holds or grows as the background warps inward. Counter-zoom is the point: size and space disagree.
p: Dolly in while zooming out on [Subject] so size holds or grows as space warps.

d: A dolly zoom out retreats on wheels while the lens zooms in, the figure shrinking or holding while space yawns. The background stretches away; the face can stay as the room leaves.
p: Dolly out while zooming in on [Subject], background stretching away.

d: A double dolly shot moves performer and camera together on one rolling platform so their relative arrangement stays fixed. The actor appears to glide rather than walk: feet skating, weight transfer absent.
p: A detective stands completely still, feet planted, while she and the camera glide forward together down a long corridor. Her face stays the same size and position. Background moves smoothly backward. No walking cycle, no bobbing, no flying pose, solemn inevitability.

d: A Dutch roll rotates the camera around the lens axis over time, so a level horizon becomes a canted one. Unease arrives as a move, not as a frozen Dutch still.
p: The camera slowly rolls, tilting the horizon around [Subject] into a Dutch angle.

d: An earth zoom is a continuous or apparently continuous rush from satellite scale down to a face, continent to street to person. Nested geography collapses along one axis; a smooth zoom is not proof of real travel speed.
p: Begin on a dew drop on one leaf. Pull backward continuously through the garden, neighborhood, coastline and cloud layer, ending above the planet. Keep one coherent outward axis, smooth logarithmic-feeling changes in scale and consistent daylight. Build as matched scale segments with composited handoffs; no random galaxy substitutions.

d: An eating zoom is a crash into the bite, chopsticks or spoon as the last foreground, appetite as a punch-in. The move is optical and short; the dish should be nameable in the last frame.
p: Crash zoom into [Subject] taking a bite, food and mouth filling the frame.

d: An eyes in camera push travels into the gaze until the irises own the frame. It does not stop at a close-up; the portrait becomes an interior of sclera, iris, and catchlight.
p: The camera pushes into [Subject]

d: An FPV drone shot is first-person aerial flying: the camera banks, dives, and threads architecture at high speed. It is proximity and flight, a racing craft with a lens, not a slow crane and not a high establishing hover.
p: FPV drone flies past and around [Subject] with banking turns and proximity to structures.

d: A falling camera drops the lens through air with weight and wind, a body or viewpoint in free fall. Gravity is the path: the ground rises, air rushes, and the horizon may not stay polite.
p: The camera falls with [Subject], rushing air, ground rising, six seconds of drop.

d: A fixed camera locks position and tilt so all motion belongs to the world, not the operator. The mount does not pan, tilt, or travel; blocking has to finish the shot.
p: Camera locked. Only [Subject] and the air move.

d: A flying cam transition is one continuous flight that punches a wall or window and lands in a new room. Architecture becomes a tunnel; the join is travel, not a hidden cut.
p: The camera flies through architecture around [Subject], passing a threshold into a new space.

d: A follow shot trails a moving subject at a fixed offset, usually from behind. The back of the head becomes foreground and the world opens ahead, so pursuit, haunting, or arrival is felt as walking into space.
p: The camera follows behind [Subject], matching their movement through the space.

d: A gimbal shot uses motorized stabilization for smooth handheld or vehicle-mounted movement. Electronic inertia damps roll and high-frequency shake while a human still carries the camera, freer than a dolly and cleaner than raw handheld.
p: Smooth gimbal move following [Subject], stabilized but slightly human, gliding through the space.

d: A handheld camera is operated from the body without a stabilizing vest or gimbal, so breathing, micro-shake, and mass stay in the frame. The image has the nerves of a person holding weight, not a track and not a motor.
p: Inside a moving minibus, a compact camera pivots from two chatting passengers to the windscreen as a fallen tree blocks the road, then to the driver’s reaction and the rear window. One continuous-looking viewpoint, consistent seats, believable window parallax, restrained panic. Build separate interior and exterior plates when necessary.

d: A head tracking camera glues the lens to the skull so the face stays pinned while the background orbits. The head is the tripod; turns shear the room.
p: The camera stays locked to [Subject]

d: Hero cam is a low three-quarter tracking walk with rim light, a comic-book arrival at walking speed. The recipe is height plus travel plus a hard edge of light, not a static low angle.
p: Low heroic tracking on [Subject] walking, rim light, mythic pace.

d: A hyperlapse combines time-lapse with significant camera movement through space. Time is compressed while the camera advances in steps that assemble into a glide, so crowds and weather race along a real path.
p: Hyperlapse: the camera advances through the space around [Subject] while time is compressed, clouds and traffic racing.

d: A jib down camera is a short descending arm, a few feet of boom, intimate arrival with nearby foreground sliding as the camera sits down. It is a small crane, not a city-scale drop.
p: A short jib down into [Subject], small crane, the room arriving rather than a city-scale drop.

d: A jib shot uses a short pivoting arm to raise, lower, or sweep the camera a few feet. It is a compact crane: small height change, often over a table, a walk, or a two-shot.
p: A compact jib arm lifts a few feet above [Subject] with a gentle sweep.

d: A jib up camera is a short rising arm that gives a table or face back to the room, human-scale lift. Who else is present appears; a skyline does not have to.
p: A short jib up from [Subject], revealing who else is in the room.

d: A lazy susan shot rotates the subject on a motorized turntable while the camera stays put, or the camera circles at a fixed product-hero radius. Distance holds, so scale does not change, and the far wall barely shears if the disc is what turns.
p: [Subject] rotates slowly as if on a turntable, or the camera circles at product-hero distance.

d: A locked-on shot keeps one object or face glued in frame while the world streams past, as if the camera were bolted to a vehicle, a fall, or a spinning set. The subject is the only stable point.
p: The camera stays locked on [Subject] while the environment streams past them.

d: A mouth in camera move enters speech or appetite until lips and teeth become the set. The camera travels past the portrait into the orifice as landscape.
p: The camera pushes into [Subject]

d: Omnidirectional capture uses a 360 camera to record spherical space, so the viewer can look any way and there is no behind the camera. Off-screen ceases to exist as a hiding place.
p: A 360-degree world around [Subject], camera able to look anywhere.

d: A pan shot rotates the camera horizontally around a fixed position, yaw on the vertical axis, feet planted. The support does not travel; the horizon should stay level as the frame sweeps the world.
p: Two siblings argue quietly at a kitchen table. Hold a two-shot; when one stands, gently tilt and pan to include her without cutting. As she leans back toward the seated brother, settle into a tighter shared composition. No arbitrary camera movement.

d: A pan left is pan shot cinematography that rotates the camera on a fixed tripod or head around its vertical axis, sweeping the view to the left. The support does not travel; only the direction of the lens changes.
p: The camera pans left from a fixed tripod, sweeping across [Subject] and the environment. No body travel.

d: A pan right shot is a horizontal rotation of a locked-off camera toward the right. It connects two parts of the same geography in one continuous turn from a single station point.
p: The camera pans right from a fixed tripod across [Subject]. Smooth horizontal rotation only.

d: Parallax cinematography is the relative apparent motion between near and far objects as the camera translates. Near things race, far things crawl; that speed difference is how the image proves the world has layers.
p: Camera moves so foreground around [Subject] slides faster than the background.

d: A camera pass through travels through a wall, a body, or a window as if matter were optional. The path is continuous: one side of the barrier, its thickness, then the next space, without a cut.
p: The camera passes through architecture or [Subject] into the next space.

d: A pedestal down lowers the entire camera vertically without changing its tilt. The descent stays on one axis: a calm drop through the same look, not a nod and not a crane swoop.
p: The camera lowers straight down on a pedestal, keeping tilt constant, settling onto [Subject].

d: A pedestal shot moves the entire camera vertically without changing its tilt. The lens rises on a column, eyeline climbs, and architecture slides down the frame while pitch stays constant.
p: The camera rises straight up on a pedestal, keeping the same tilt, lifting past [Subject].

d: A pull out shot moves physically or virtually away from the subject so more environment enters around a person or detail. Intimacy widens into context without changing lenses.
p: Slow pull out from [Subject], the frame widening to reveal the environment.

d: A push in shot moves physically or virtually closer to the subject so size grows because the camera walks. It is a short pressure advance, often so gradual the audience feels the walls close before they notice motion.
p: Very slow push in toward [Subject] over 6 seconds, medium into medium close-up.

d: A rapid zoom in snaps focal length faster than a polite crash, almost a cut, the world tightening in a few frames, then a hold. The camera body does not travel.
p: Extremely fast zoom into [Subject], nearly a cut, then a hold.

d: A rapid zoom out snaps from the subject to a wide, the environment exploding into view, then holds. Reveal as shock or joke; the camera body still does not travel.
p: Snap zoom out from [Subject] to a wide, then hold.

d: A road rush camera sits low to the asphalt, speed as smear, headlights and lane lines as weapons. The road is the subject; a vehicle is optional.
p: Low camera rushing along the road with [Subject], speed blur, lane lines streaking.

d: A robotic camera arm runs a programmed path with inhuman precision, repeatable every take for product geometry or a stunt match. No operator shake; the spline is the performance.
p: A precise robotic-arm path around [Subject], repeatable, no human shake.

d: A slider shot is a short, precise linear move on a compact rail, often 60 to 120 centimeters. It adds parallax to an interview, product, or lock-off without a full dolly track.
p: A short slider move laterally across [Subject], subtle parallax, 6 seconds.

d: A slow zoom in is slow zoom in cinematography that tightens the frame by increasing focal length while the camera body stays locked. Perspective relations stay fixed: the world does not slide, it only enlarges as the lens compresses space.
p: From a distant fixed window, slowly zoom into a solitary woman waiting at the center of a city square. Eight seconds, no camera translation, no foreground parallax, patient observational mood. She never acknowledges the camera.

d: A slow zoom out widens the frame by decreasing focal length while the support stays put. More architecture and negative space enter the picture, yet the camera never travels, so true parallax does not appear.
p: The lens slowly zooms out for 6 seconds from a tight frame on [Subject] into a wider environment. Camera body stays still.

d: A SnorriCam fixes the camera to the performer's body so the body remains stable relative to frame while the world moves. A rig points back at the wearer: the face stays pinned, the environment pitches around it.
p: A frightened commuter walks quickly through a tiled tunnel. Body-mounted camera facing him: face and shoulders stay locked in the center while the corridor tilts and bobs with every step. Wide-angle proximity, natural strain, no free camera orbit and no normal handheld tracking.

d: A static locked-off shot plants the camera on a heavy tripod with zero camera movement. Composition, blocking, and duration do the work; the frame is a living picture that does not tour.
p: In a dark archive, a librarian listens for someone outside. Remove music entirely and retain only quiet ventilation, cloth movement and her restrained breathing. Let the ventilation stop, leaving a single distant latch click clearly exposed. No sudden monster reveal or oversized bass hit.

d: Steadicam is a mechanical stabilizing system using a sled, arm, and vest, so an operator can walk while the camera floats. The path can connect rooms with a smoothness that is neither handheld tremor nor dolly traction.
p: Smooth Steadicam move floating with [Subject] through the environment, no footfall shake.

d: A super dolly in is a long aggressive travel that eats the room, parallax violent, the face arriving too fast. It is a dolly in stretched until geography collapses into a close-up in one move.
p: A long, fast dolly in toward [Subject], the room collapsing into a close-up.

d: A super dolly out is a long retreat that dumps the person into geography, the room exploding open. The environment takes the frame; the figure is left inside a system they no longer fill.
p: A long, fast dolly out from [Subject] until the environment owns the frame.

d: Through object in sends the camera into a cup, keyhole, speaker, or mouth, matter as a door, then arrives on the subject. Scale often changes along a coherent 3D route that a physical camera could not take.
p: A single virtual camera glides from a dark kitchen, through the narrow handle opening of a kettle, across the room and through a keyhole into a lit study. Rigid continuous architecture, physically coherent perspective, controlled acceleration, no melting surfaces. Previsualize the route in 3D and use generated textures or plates rather than relying on one unconstrained generation.

d: Through object out leaves the subject by traveling out through an object into a wider world, interior becoming exterior. The viewpoint can abandon the person and let the decisive event happen off its direct attention.
p: Begin inside a quiet hotel room with a traveler seated near the edge of frame. Slowly approach a barred window, pass beyond it without visible interruption, drift into the courtyard, then turn to look back at the room. The traveler remains offscreen during a muffled disturbance. Use a planned barrier-removal composite, not bending metal.

d: A tilt shot rotates the camera vertically around a fixed position, pitch on the horizontal axis, tripod planted. Height is revealed or hidden by angle, not by lifting the support.
p: The camera tilts vertically across [Subject], tripod planted.

d: A tilt-down rotates the camera vertically from a fixed position, starting higher and ending lower. It can drop from sky or architecture onto a person or object without moving the tripod.
p: The camera tilts down from above onto [Subject], revealing the figure from head to environment.

d: A tilt up shot rotates the camera vertically around a fixed position, climbing from a lower composition to a higher one. The tripod does not rise; only pitch changes, so the viewpoint height stays the same.
p: Begin on a small muddy shoe at the foot of a massive stone monument. Slowly tilt upward from the same fixed position, revealing a child standing on a ledge high above. Maintain believable vertical lines, no crane rise, no zoom.

d: A tracking shot moves with, beside, ahead of, or behind a moving subject, typically matching pace on a parallel path. The person supplies the motion; the camera keeps distance, height, and scale while foreground, mid-ground, and deep background peel.
p: Side-on continuous shot of a tired security guard trying to pass three obstructing figures in a narrow service corridor. Choreographed non-graphic action, visible pauses and fatigue, full bodies readable, camera tracks only laterally. No rapid edits, no impossible acrobatics, no concealed geography.

d: A trucking shot is a lateral dolly: the camera slides sideways with a walker, a sidewalk or corridor peeling by. Subject size holds; the world streams along the street axis.
p: The camera trucks sideways with [Subject], lateral parallax.

d: A walk and talk shot moves with speaking people, camera leading or flanking at medium, so information and geography travel together. Architecture flows while a moving two-shot (or a moving single with interruptions) carries the dialogue.
p: The camera leads [Subject] walking through a space, holding a moving medium two-shot energy even if one figure.

d: A wandering camera drifts near the subject as curiosity, a search without a target yet. The move is not a motivated reframe to a known fact; looking itself is the action until something is found.
p: The camera wanders through the space around [Subject], discovering rather than targeting.

d: A whip pan pans so quickly that the image blurs into horizontal streaks, then snaps to a new composition. Two shots can be joined inside compatible directional motion blur, creating the impression of one fast reorientation.
p: Generate A: a baker turns toward a ringing telephone and the camera whip-pans right into horizontal blur. Generate B: begin with the same rightward blur and land on a flour-covered delivery driver outside. Join at maximum blur. Keep motion direction and brightness compatible; no dissolve.

d: A whip tilt is a violent, motion-blurred vertical rotation of the camera, then a hard stop. It is the up-or-down cousin of a whip pan: shock through speed, not through traveling the support.
p: Extremely fast vertical whip tilt across [Subject] with motion blur, then a hard stop.

d: A wiggle camera rocks between two nearby viewpoints, a tiny stereo fidget that makes a lock-off read as a living postcard. Travel is centimeters, not a dolly.
p: The camera wiggles between two nearby viewpoints of [Subject].

d: A yoyo zoom inhales and exhales on the optical axis: a punch then a release, camera body still. One breath, two directions, no dolly.
p: The lens zooms in then out on [Subject] in one breath, a yo-yo on the optical axis.

d: A zoom shot changes focal length without moving the camera. Space flattens or opens with no parallax: near and far grow or shrink together because the nodal point stays put.
p: The lens zooms on [Subject], no camera travel, space compressing.

d: A choker shot, also called a big close-up (BCU), frames the face from hairline to chin, often clipping the skull on every side. Shoulders are out; almost no background remains.
p: Choker shot of [Subject] from hairline to chin, almost no background, claustrophobic portrait, Bergman proximity.

d: A close-up, or close up shot, frames a face tightly enough to privilege detail over surroundings, usually head and upper shoulders. The room becomes secondary; the person still reads as a head, not a fragment.
p: Tight close-up of [Subject], head and upper shoulders, shallow depth of field, creamy bokeh, 75mm Cooke, the face as landscape.

d: A cowboy shot frames a person from mid-thigh or the knees upward so the hands stay in at the holster line. It is also called an American shot or knee shot; it is not a waist shot and not a full figure.
p: Cowboy shot of [Subject] framed mid-thigh up, hands visible at the holster line, American shot, casual authority.

d: A cut-in, or cut in shot, moves from a wider view to a closer detail of something already present in that space, usually along the same axis. It proves a fact the wide cannot prove: the hands, the phone, the wound.
p: Cut-in on a detail of [Subject] already in the master, tighter, the same axis, a fact the wide cannot prove.

d: A cutaway shot leaves the primary action for a related detail, observer, or part of the same world. It is used for context, reaction, compression, or continuity repair.
p: A couple argues quietly in a kitchen. Cut away to a kettle beginning to tremble on the stove while their voices continue, then return to the couple after a tense pause. Generate the insert separately with matching light and room sound. No literal symbolism captions.

d: An establishing shot introduces or re-establishes location, geography, time of day, or social context. It is a job in the sequence, not a synonym for wide or extreme long shot.
p: After a daughter leaves the house, hold a static shot of the empty entryway: her shoes are gone, afternoon light remains on the floor and distant street noise continues. No person enters, no camera move, no sentimental insert music. Cut to the next scene only after the room has registered as its own space.

d: An extreme close-up, or extreme close up shot, fills the frame with one small feature: an eye, a mouth, a fingertip, a trigger. Surrounding space disappears; the crop is tighter than a whole face.
p: Extreme close-up of an older watchmaker’s eyes as she decides whether to open a sealed mechanism. Frame from brow to upper cheek, natural skin texture, tiny shift in gaze and controlled breathing. Restrained light, stable focus, no cosmetic smoothing or wide-angle facial distortion.

d: An extreme long shot makes environment, scale, geography, or isolation dominant over individual detail. A person, if present, is a speck: a scale mark, not a portrait.
p: Extreme-wide static shot of a lone surveyor in a yellow coat at the base of an enormous concrete spillway. The figure is tiny but unmistakable; immense walls recede naturally. Slow drifting mist, no camera move, no giant-person scale errors.

d: A full body shot holds a person head to toe, with the figure complete and a readable strip of environment around the silhouette. The person is still the subject; the world is a border, not the owner of the frame.
p: Full-body shot of [Subject], head to toe, figure complete in frame, environment readable around the silhouette.

d: Gesture cinematography sizes and times a shot around a discrete expressive body movement: a hand, a glance, a weight shift. The plot is in the motion, not in an object sitting still.
p: Gesture close on [Subject], the meaning in a hand, a glance, a weight shift, coverage of the small action.

d: A group shot frames a small ensemble as a relational unit, such as a family, a crew, or a jury. Position, height, and light say who belongs and who dominates.
p: Group shot containing [Subject] among several figures, ensemble blocking, who owns the frame by position and light.

d: An insert shot is a close view of a story-relevant detail: an object, a hand action, a screen, or text. It points at the thing that will matter, at real scale.
p: Outline a short caper around an unopened blue envelope sought by three strangers. Never reveal its contents. Build the scenes around shifting trust, mistaken possession and one character choosing a friend over the envelope. Generate a consistent, easily trackable prop for every shot.

d: Interview cinematography is a talking-head setup: stable size, eyeline just off the lens, a listener implied. Someone is answering a question we often do not hear.
p: Interview frame of [Subject], talking-head distance, eyeline just off lens, a listener implied.

d: A long shot in cinematography shows the full subject plus a substantial portion of the environment, so a person sits small in geography. The figure is still locatable as a human; the world is large enough to ignore them.
p: Long shot of [Subject] small in a large environment, full figure plus geography, mythic placement of a person in land.

d: A master shot covers the complete dramatic action and the spatial geography of a scene in one setup. It is the skeleton you can play in full, then cut into.
p: Wide master of [Subject] with all blocking visible, the skeleton of the scene in one continuous frame, coverage can cut in later.

d: A medium close-up, or medium close up, usually frames a person from chest or shoulders upward. Dialogue distance remains: face, shoulders, and often a hand at chest height stay readable.
p: Medium close-up of [Subject] from chest up, dialogue distance, shoulders and hands still readable, 65 to 75mm.

d: A medium shot frames a person from approximately the waist upward, so face and gesture share the rectangle. It is the workhorse size of coverage, sometimes called a waist shot.
p: Medium shot of [Subject] from the waist up, conversational distance, 50mm, gesture and face in balance.

d: Over-the-shoulder coverage, or an over the shoulder shot, puts a near shoulder or head in the foreground while the far face stays sharp. Paired reverses preserve relational space.
p: Generate two matching over-the-shoulder shots of a tense café conversation. A: the man’s blurred shoulder frames the woman’s face. B: her blurred shoulder frames his face. Preserve seat positions, cup placement and light direction. Edit on changing reactions, not every spoken word.

d: Product cinematography lights and frames an object the way a portrait treats a face: hero angle, catalog clarity, controlled reflections. The thing is the subject, not a plot insert in a messy room.
p: Product hero of [Subject], catalog clarity, controlled reflections, the object as celebrity.

d: A reaction shot shows a character's response to an event, a line, or an unseen stimulus. The important action is watching; the face (or body) is the cut.
p: Generate one neutral close-up of a woman looking slightly down and right. Reuse the identical clip in three short edits: after a broken heirloom, after a sleeping puppy and after an unsigned contract. Generate the inserts separately and keep the reaction genuinely unchanged. Compare the meanings created by the juxtaposition.

d: A single, in single shot cinematography, is a coverage shot of one principal character, not a one-take scene. A clean single keeps other bodies out; a dirty single lets a shoulder or blur from the partner chew the edge without becoming a true over-the-shoulder.
p: Clean single of [Subject], one person, no foreground shoulder, the frame belonging entirely to them.

d: A three-shot, or three shot, frames three principal subjects together, usually so alliances and the odd one out are readable in the blocking. It is a group sentence of three, not three singles cut together.
p: Three-shot of [Subject] in a triangular group, alliances and the odd one out readable in blocking.

d: A two-shot, or two shot, frames two principal subjects together so their distance and posture can be compared in one composition. The space between them is part of the sentence.
p: Hold a medium profile two-shot of two former business partners seated across a narrow café table. Both faces remain readable at once. One leans forward while the other slowly leans back. No cutting to singles, no focus change, tension expressed through changing distance.

d: A video portrait is a sustained, simply covered study of one person: stable size, patient time, the face as the whole event. Duration is the intimacy; a person is enough.
p: A long held portrait of [Subject], tiny life in the face, almost still.

d: A wide shot shows the subject in full environment, with bodies small enough that place still speaks. It is environment-forward coverage: do not isolate yet.
p: Wide shot of [Subject] in full environment, bodies small enough that place still speaks.

d: A bird's-eye view shot looks steeply or directly down from a great height so people and furniture become a map. Height, not just distance, is the point of view: life reads as a board game or a ritual seen from above.
p: Bird

d: A Dutch angle rolls the camera so verticals and the horizon appear tilted. The cant is usually static: gravity's down is no longer the bottom of the frame, which is why the world reads as off its axis.
p: A tenant confronts a landlord in a narrow stairwell. Static camera canted fifteen degrees, strong diagonal banister, rigid walls and natural anatomy. Both actors remain grounded. No rolling camera, fisheye distortion or vibrating image; the tension comes from the tilted composition.

d: An eye-level shot places the camera at the subject's eye height with a horizontal sightline and a level horizon. It is the default equal relationship: height and tilt assign no rank until you leave this setup.
p: Eye-level shot of [Subject], camera at their eye height, horizontal sightline, equal relationship, no power tilt.

d: A first-person camera makes the lens function as a character's bodily viewpoint, with a body that owns it: hands entering the frame, breath, tools, locomotion. It is subjective seeing as continuous embodiment, not a single optical insert.
p: First-person view moving as [Subject] moves, hands or tools entering the edges.

d: A fourth-wall look aims the subject's eyes into the taking lens, so the scene admits an audience. The camera is no longer an invisible observer; it is a person in the room, or the spectator the character has decided to include.
p: A meticulous traveler narrates how carefully she plans every journey while the images show her repeatedly improvising: borrowing a map, following a stranger’s gesture and boarding at the last moment. Write restrained original narration that reveals self-image through contradiction rather than explaining visible actions.

d: A ground-level shot puts the lens almost on the floor, so boots, hems, wheels, and the dirt become actors. Height is the fact: the camera starts from the ground plane, whether it looks along the street or steeply up.
p: Ground-level camera looking steeply up at [Subject], lens nearly on the floor, boots and trailing coat monumental.

d: A high-angle shot looks downward at the subject from above eye level, an oblique pitch rather than a straight drop. More floor enters the frame, the figure occupies less of the rectangle, and the viewpoint reads as observation from above.
p: High oblique view of a lone cleaner crossing a vast empty railway hall after midnight. The architecture and floor pattern dominate. The cleaner pauses at a distant sound. Fixed elevated viewpoint, no drone swoop or zoom.

d: A hip-level shot sits the camera around belt or holster height so hands, gait, and weapons share the plane of focus. It is a height choice, usually with a level horizon: the hands will decide.
p: Hip-level camera on [Subject], gunbelt height, Western stance, hands and holster in the plane of focus.

d: An incline is a slight camera roll, a gentle cant of the floor rather than a full Dutch angle. The horizon is a few degrees off true, enough to suggest slope or unease without declaring that the world has fallen over.
p: Inclined camera on [Subject], a gentle cant, not a full Dutch, the floor suggesting slope or unease.

d: A low-angle shot looks upward at the subject from below eye level, so verticals converge and ceilings or sky take weight. The camera is not merely low; it is pitched up, and that pitch is what assigns monument or intimidation.
p: A quiet family conversation in a modest room, filmed from a low seated height with the camera level. Two adults sit beside a low table, doorways carefully balanced, no dramatic upward angle. Locked shot, small natural gestures, patient pauses.

d: An object-POV shot is the viewpoint of a tool, a ball, a bullet, a phone, or a vehicle: the prop has eyes. The camera is parented to that object, so the object stays stable in the frame while the world moves relative to it.
p: Camera rigidly attached beside the front fork of an old bicycle, looking ahead. The fork stays fixed in the lower-left frame while cobblestones rush beneath and street corners swing with the steering. Real wheel rotation and restrained mechanical vibration; no detached drone movement.

d: An overhead top-down shot looks nearly straight down at 90 degrees, flattening bodies and spaces into a graphic arrangement. Faces are scarce; silhouette, props, and the plan of the table or room do the talking.
p: Strict top-down locked shot of four people setting a long table, their hands passing plates in a coordinated pattern. The tabletop forms a clean rectangle, no perspective tilt, no camera rotation. One person stops and the system loses its rhythm.

d: A POV shot makes the camera function as a character's optical viewpoint: what they see at their eye height. The looker's head and shoulder stay out of the frame; we inhabit the look, not a seat behind it.
p: At a crowded celebration, a character becomes overwhelmed. Keep the image continuous while voices lose clarity, room detail recedes and a small nearby glass movement becomes unusually prominent. Return gradually to the room when a friend touches her shoulder. Build the perceptual transition in sound post-production.

d: A profile shot places the camera at 90 degrees to the head so one ear, the jaw, and the nose read as architecture, with the look offscreen. It is a true side view, not a three-quarter face and not a stamped coin if the living head still breathes.
p: True profile of [Subject], camera at 90 degrees to the head, one ear, the nose as architecture, looking offscreen. A human face, not a stamped portrait.

d: A reverse-angle shot views the same spatial relationship from the opposing side, completing the axis of a look, a dialogue, or a standoff. Geography flips; the 180-degree line is respected so screen direction still matches.
p: Close-up of a caretaker opening a basement door just outside frame. Her expression changes as she sees something below, but hold on her face and the dark edge of the doorway. A quiet mechanical clicking comes from downstairs. Never cut to what she sees during this shot.

d: A shoulder-level camera sits slightly below the eyes, at the height of a walking companion. It is less formal than true eye level and less monumental than a low angle; the face is still the target, seen from the deltoid rather than the pupil.
p: Shoulder-level camera on [Subject], slightly below the eyes, a walking companion

d: A three-quarter angle turns the face about 45 degrees to the camera so both eyes remain visible and the far cheek recedes. It is the standard narrative portrait angle: dimensionality without a full front or a true side.
p: Three-quarter angle on [Subject], face turned about 45 degrees, classic portrait dimensionality.

d: A trunk shot places the camera inside a car trunk or similar confined pit, looking up at the people who open it, with the lid and rim framing their downward looks. It is a located low viewpoint, not a generic look-up in a parking lot.
p: From inside an old wooden instrument case, look upward as two conservators open the lid and lean over it. The dark case rim frames their faces against a bright workshop ceiling. Clear lid movement, coherent downward eyelines, no camera rise or reveal of the observer.

d: A worm's-eye view looks sharply upward from ground level or below the subject, an extreme low pitch that collapses verticals inward. The subject is a tower and the camera is dust.
p: Worm

d: Available light in available light cinematography is the illumination already at the location before the crew adds or changes units: sun, sky, or existing interior fixtures. You commit to the hour and the existing contrast.
p: Available light only on [Subject], sun, sky, or existing interior fixtures, documentary humility, no added units.

d: Backlight in backlight cinematography is light coming from behind the subject toward the camera, tracing edges and lifting the figure off the background. It may stay a thin rim or, in haze, become a visible shaft.
p: A conservator enters a dark archive where one high window sends a narrow hard shaft through suspended dust. Her body briefly interrupts the beam, producing a coherent moving shadow in the haze. Deep room, restrained atmosphere, no magical glowing particles.

d: Blue hour in blue hour cinematography is cool ambient twilight before sunrise or after sunset, when the sun is below the horizon but the sky still glows. There is no hard sunlight; the sky is a large cool source, and warm practicals often kick in.
p: Blue hour wrap on [Subject], deep cobalt sky still glowing, warm practicals kicking in, Mann twilight melancholy.

d: Bounce lighting reflects light from a surface (wall, ceiling, poly, card) before it reaches the subject, so the apparent source becomes that large surface. Direction remains, but shadow edges soften and wrap.
p: Bounce light on [Subject], key ricocheted off a white wall or poly, wrapping, gentle, large-source softness.

d: Broad lighting keys the side of the face turned toward camera, so the near cheek is the bright one and the shadow sits on the far side. The face reads open, public, and less mysterious.
p: Broad lighting on [Subject], the camera-facing side keyed, open and public, less shadow on the near cheek.

d: Butterfly lighting, also called Paramount lighting, places the key high and on the camera axis so a small butterfly-shaped shadow falls under the nose on the philtrum. Both cheeks stay open; both eyes take light.
p: Key light high and centered on [Subject]

d: Cameo lighting isolates a lit subject against a predominantly dark environment, so the figure sits in a pool and the world falls to black. The person remains modeled; the set is withheld.
p: Cameo lighting on [Subject], figure isolated in a pool against a black void, theatrical spotlight, no environment.

d: Candlelight in candlelight cinematography is a small warm practical or a simulated flame with rapid falloff, often around 1800K, that carves faces near the flame and lets the rest of the room die. Flicker is part of the source, not a grade.
p: An eighteenth-century card game lit as if only by clustered candles on the table. Faces fade quickly into darkness with distance from the flames, warm uneven illumination, believable flame detail and subdued room corners. A slow restrained gesture, no bright modern fill or electric orange wash.

d: Chiaroscuro lighting uses strong light-dark contrast to model volume and to create moral, psychological, or dramatic tension. Darkness withholds; the lit plane is what the scene will admit.
p: A tailor listens to an uneasy visitor in a dim back room. One high window shapes half the tailor’s face; the rest falls into deep but readable shadow. Warm desk practical in the distance, no even beauty fill, no crushed featureless blacks.

d: Cross lighting keys subjects from opposite side directions, so each person or each side of a body gets a key and a far rim. It is common in dialogue coverage, stage, and concert work.
p: Cross lighting on [Subject] from two opposing keys, dual rims, theatrical or concert energy, edges on both sides.

d: Dappled light is broken patches of brightness and shadow caused by foliage, water, blinds, or another irregular obstruction in a hard beam. The pattern is organic and often moving.
p: Sun through leaves on [Subject], irregular patches of brightness and leaf-shaped shadows on coat and horse, a real tree overhead.

d: Epiphany lighting is a change of illumination that makes a face or figure suddenly the brightest readable fact in the room as a realization lands. The light finds the person; it is timed to understanding, not left as a static setup.
p: Light finds [Subject] as a realization lands, the face becoming the brightest fact in the room.

d: An eye light in eye light cinematography is a small frontal source used to put a catchlight in the irises or to lift the eyes a fraction without becoming a fill. The face can stay in shadow; the eyes remain human, not lamps.
p: A dark portrait of [Subject], face mostly in shadow, a tiny white reflection of a lamp sitting in each human iris. Eyes stay brown or grey, not glowing.

d: Fill light reduces contrast or adds detail in areas the key does not reach, usually from the opposite side and at a lower level. It is a ratio tool, not a second sun.
p: Soft fill light opening the shadow side of [Subject] without flattening, a low ratio that keeps eyes alive.

d: Glam lighting, in glam lighting terms, is a large beauty key with catchlights in the eyes and a little diffusion on skin, built to sell the face. It is a package of size, frontal or near-frontal placement, and skin treatment, not a single nose-shadow pattern.
p: Soft beauty key on [Subject], large source, catchlights inside the eyes, a little diffusion on skin. No projected squares or grids on the face.

d: Gobo lighting places a pattern or object in a light beam (a gobo or cucoloris) so the source throws graphic shadows across face, body, and wall. The room writes on the person.
p: Gobo-patterned light on [Subject], venetian blinds, bars, or branches throwing graphic shadows across face and wall.

d: Golden hour in golden hour cinematography is low-angle warm sunlight shortly after sunrise or before sunset, when the sun is near the horizon. Shadows go long; the light is directional, warm, and brief.
p: Two farm workers walk beside a wheat field just after sunset. Soft luminous sky, low contrast on their faces, warm remnants on the horizon, no direct overhead sun. Gentle wind and patient lateral movement, natural exposure, no exaggerated orange filter.

d: A hair light is a small source behind and above the subject that lights only the top of the hair as a rim so texture separates from the background. The face stays on the key or in cooler shadow.
p: A small lamp behind and above [Subject], lighting only the top of the hair as a rim. The face stays in cooler shadow.

d: Hard light in hard light cinematography comes from a small apparent source and produces crisp shadow edges and specular definition on skin, metal, and walls. Texture is amplified; falloff can still be steep or long depending on distance.
p: Hard light on [Subject] from a small distant source, razor shadow edges, texture amplified, noir graphic.

d: High-key lighting, or high key lighting, uses relatively low contrast, bright exposure, and limited deep shadow so the frame stays open and readable. It is a contrast ratio, not a command to overexpose.
p: A meticulously cheerful pastry shop at midday, soft broad light, luminous pastel walls and gentle shadows. The owner stands motionless while everyone else smiles. High-key image with preserved white icing texture, no blown highlights or glossy skin.

d: A key light in key light cinematography is the principal source that sets the subject's dominant direction, shape, and exposure. Shadows fall away from it; every other light is measured against it.
p: Strong directional key light on [Subject] from a single defined source, the brightest storyteller in the frame, shadows as composition.

d: A kicker light is a relatively hard side-back accent on cheek, jaw, shoulder, or an object edge, placed behind and to one side of the subject. It is a slice, not a full wrap and not a hair-only rim.
p: A small warm lamp behind and to the side of [Subject], a thin highlight on the far jaw and coat shoulder only. No beam shooting out of the body.

d: Loop lighting creates a small nose shadow that loops toward the corner of the mouth and does not connect to the cheek shadow. The key sits slightly off axis and a little high, a middle step between butterfly and Rembrandt.
p: Loop lighting on [Subject], key slightly off-axis, a small loop shadow from the nose toward the corner of the mouth.

d: Low-key lighting, or low key lighting, uses high contrast, selective illumination, and substantial shadow so most of the frame can sit near black. One pool of light is often enough; the dark is designed, not an accident of underexposure.
p: Low-key lighting on [Subject], most of the frame in deep shadow, one pool of light, 8:1 contrast, noir darkness as a character.

d: Motivated lighting is designed to appear consistent with a visible or plausible story-world source: a window, a lamp, a sign, the sky. Hidden units may exist, but they match that source in direction, hardness, and color.
p: A solemn traveler crosses an empty plaza accompanied by an original elegant string theme. Pan slowly to reveal a small string quartet following him on a wheeled platform, still playing the exact phrase. Their presence is treated matter-of-factly. Generate the visual reveal and synchronize an original performance in the edit.

d: Naturalistic ambient lighting wraps the subject in soft, directionally plausible room or sky tone so the craft reads as unstyled even when units are added. Shadows stay believable; nothing announces a movie lamp.
p: Naturalistic ambient wrap on [Subject], soft room tone, believable shadow, window-motivated without theatricality.

d: Neon practicals are visible neon or similar sign tubes used as actual keys or strong accents, coloring the subject with magenta, cyan, or other tube hues instead of a hidden white source. The city fixture is the lamp.
p: Neon practicals coloring [Subject], magenta and cyan signs as real keys, wet bounce, mixed gels, night-city chromatics.

d: Practical lighting uses a visible or logically present light source within the set as a real contributor: lamps, neon, candles, screens. You see the fixture, and it (or a unit matching it) actually lights the face.
p: Practical lighting on [Subject] from visible lamps, neon, candles, or screens in frame, mixed color temperatures, no hidden movie lights.

d: Rembrandt lighting, in rembrandt lighting terms, is a portrait pattern in which the key sits high and about 45 degrees off axis so the nose shadow joins the shadow cheek, leaving a small triangle of light under the shadow-side eye. The rest of that cheek stays dark.
p: Key light high and 45 degrees on [Subject], the near cheek in light, a small triangle of light on the shadow-side cheek, the rest of that cheek dark.

d: Rim lighting is a narrow edge of light, usually from a flagged backlight, that separates a subject from the background without opening the face. The highlight sits on brim, hair, and coat; flesh stays mostly dark.
p: Photographic backlight on [Subject] from behind, a thin natural highlight on hat brim, hair, and coat edge, faces staying dark. Not a neon outline.

d: Short lighting in short lighting terms keys the side of the face turned away from camera, so the camera sees more shadow than light. The head looks slimmer and more dimensional because the near cheek falls off.
p: Short lighting on [Subject], the side turned away from camera is keyed, the near side falls toward shadow, slimming and dramatic.

d: Side lighting keys primarily from one side, around 90 degrees to the camera-subject line, so shape and texture are emphasized. Half the form goes toward light, half toward shadow.
p: Pure side light at 90 degrees on [Subject], half the face brilliant, half gone, texture and duality.

d: A silhouette shot places the subject dark against a brighter background so the figure reads as shape, not as a modeled face. Gesture and contour do the work; surface detail is gone.
p: A parent and child carry a small telescope up a ridge at dusk, rendered as clean dark silhouettes against a luminous pale sky. Keep their limbs and the telescope distinct. Locked wide view, gentle wind, no visible facial detail or artificial rim halo.

d: Soft light in soft light cinematography comes from a large apparent source and produces gradual shadow transitions and wrap around the face or body. Speculars get larger and dimmer; texture is reduced.
p: Soft wrapping light on [Subject] from a large source, gentle shadow transitions, luminous skin, Vermeer daylight.

d: Split lighting divides the face into a lit half and a shadow half by placing the key at about 90 degrees to the nose, a vertical cut down the center line. There is no Rembrandt triangle and no loop; the far plane is largely gone.
p: Split lighting on [Subject], one half of the face in light, the other in shadow, a vertical moral cut.

d: A spotlight in spotlight cinematography is a focused, hard-edged pool from a theatrical or similar instrument, with darkness around the circle. The person is treated as an act inside that pool.
p: Spotlight on [Subject], a hard pool, theater darkness around, the person as an act.

d: Three-point lighting, the basic three point lighting setup, places a key, a fill, and a backlight so a face is modeled from one dominant side, opened in the shadows, and separated from the background. The key is brightest and sets direction; fill and back exist only as ratios against it.
p: Classic three-point lighting on [Subject]: key at 45 degrees, soft fill opening shadows, warm backlight rim, sculpted dimensionality.

d: Top lighting is illumination from directly above the subject, falling on forehead, nose bridge, and shoulders while the eye sockets and the underside of the chin go into shadow. The source is a ceiling, a rig, or a high practical, not a frontal beauty key.
p: A lamp directly above [Subject], light falling on forehead and shoulders, eye sockets in shadow, human eyes, no light emitting from the pupils.

d: Underlighting, also called uplighting, lights from below the face so shadows climb the cheekbones and the tops of the eye sockets. The modeling is the reverse of daylight and often reads as uncanny.
p: A lamp on the table below [Subject]

d: Volumetric lighting makes beams visible through haze, fog, dust, smoke, or other particles, so the air photographs as well as the subject. Also called god rays or crepuscular rays when the shafts are distinct.
p: Volumetric god rays through haze around [Subject], visible beams, dust in the shaft, cathedral or forest light as architecture.

d: Window light in window light cinematography is illumination shaped to appear as light entering through a window: a large, directional source with falloff into the room. The architecture is the modifier.
p: Window light as the only key on [Subject], large soft directional source, falloff into the room, painterly interior.

d: Architexture, a nickname for architectural cinematography that treats the set as subject, fills the frame with facades, grids, and materials until a person is a detail of the building. Texture, module, and mass own space, and the body is an ornament or a scale figure.
p: Architecture as texture around [Subject], façades, grids, and materials filling the frame until the person is a detail of the building.

d: Asymmetry, or asymmetrical composition, offsets the dominant mass and answers it with a different kind of weight: color, light, a small face, a dark void, or a distant doorway. The frame does not mirror, so leftover space is a counterweight rather than a matching wing.
p: Asymmetrical balance with [Subject] offset, counterweights of color or mass, tension instead of mirror.

d: Centered composition places the dominant subject on or near the central vertical axis and organizes the rest of the picture around that axis. The frame reads as a frontal tableau: walls, furniture, and attendants arranged so the subject is an altar, not an accident of blocking.
p: Dead-center composition of [Subject], bilateral symmetry or frontal tableau, Wes Anderson formality, the subject as altar.

d: Central framing, also called dead center or center punch, places the figure on the optical axis so the body sits on the crosshairs of the frame. Bilateral weight may gather around that body, but the first fact is placement: the person is the altar, not a guest in a third.
p: Central framing of [Subject], the figure on the optical axis, bilateral weight, a formal altar in the frame.

d: A clean frame in clean frame cinematography keeps the edges empty of accidental objects so isolation arrives by tidiness, not by blur. The diagram has no landlord in the corners, which is studio-poster clarity even on a real street.
p: Clean frame of [Subject], edges empty, no accidental objects, studio-poster clarity, isolation by tidiness.

d: Diagonal composition uses diagonal lines and masses (stairs, rifles, rain, a body on the bias, a street receding on a corner) to raise energy, instability, or depth. The camera can stay level, because the set supplies the tilt of the diagram.
p: Diagonal composition through [Subject], energy on the bias, unstable, dynamic, rain or stairs as the line.

d: A dirty frame in dirty frame cinematography lets out-of-focus shoulders, glass, foliage, or crowd chew the edges of the picture so the aperture is occupied. The camera sits inside a populated space, not on a seamless studio axis.
p: Dirty frame around [Subject], out-of-focus shoulders, glass, foliage, or crowd chewing the edges, voyeur layers.

d: Figure-ground composition separates the subject from the field so the person or object reads in under a second. Contrast of tone, color, or focus does the split, and if figure and ground share the same value the diagram fails even if the acting is good.
p: Clear figure-ground separation of [Subject] from background, contrast of tone, color, or focus so the person reads instantly.

d: Foreground interest (a foreground anchor or occluded observation) puts a salient near object between the lens and the subject: flowers, a fence, glass, a table, or a body. The near layer creates depth, scale, a visual entry, or partial concealment, so air and obstacle sit between us and them.
p: Observe two neighbors speaking softly in a stairwell through a narrow gap between a door and its frame. A dark blurred door edge occupies one third of the image. The camera remains hidden and still; both faces remain readable when they lean toward the light.

d: A frame within a frame (doorway framing, surcadrage) puts a second rectangle inside the screen, a door, window, arch, mirror, or gap that encloses the subject. The inner aperture is a second boundary, and crossing it is a beat, not a decoration.
p: From inside a dim farmhouse, hold on a bright rectangular doorway framing a lone traveler outside. The family passes into the room while the traveler remains beyond the threshold. Locked wide shot, no push-in, natural exposure contrast.

d: Golden ratio composition organizes the frame with proportional relationships near phi, about eight to five, as a phi grid or a logarithmic spiral rather than a 3x3. The main mass sits closer to center than a third, and the eye is asked to travel a curve through secondary masses instead of jumping cell to cell.
p: Golden-ratio spiral composition around [Subject], the eye traveling a harmonic curve rather than a grid.

d: Headroom in headroom cinematography is the space between the crown of the head and the top frame edge. Tight headroom applies pressure, while generous headroom hands the upper field to air, architecture, or sky.
p: Deliberate headroom on [Subject], either tight to the hair (pressure) or generously open (air, God, sky).

d: Layered depth, or layered composition, stages important action on at least two distances, typically foreground, midground, and background in one picture. Depth staging is that arrangement, while deep focus is a separate optical choice about how much of it is sharp.
p: A landlord signs a document in the near foreground while, through an open doorway, a family quietly packs in the distant room. Hold both actions in one wide composition. The foreground gesture must not obscure the family. No cut or explanatory insert.

d: Lead room in lead room cinematography (nose room, looking room) is space in the direction a subject looks or moves. More frame sits ahead of the walk or the gaze than behind the head, so the surplus is the path rather than leftover wallpaper.
p: Lead room in front of [Subject]

d: Leading lines in leading lines cinematography are edges, rails, roads, corridors, shadows, or gestures that steer the eye toward or through the image. The lines are vectors in the diagram, not decoration around a centered face.
p: Leading lines driving the eye to [Subject], rails, corridors, roads, or shadows converging on the figure.

d: Look space framing is the field in front of a gaze, the air a look owns, often because the important object is off-screen. In cutting, that look may be joined to what is seen (raccord regard, the look-object relationship).
p: Generate A: a seated woman looks upward and to her left toward a sound. Generate B: a slightly elevated wall clock seen from her seated side of the room. Generate C: return to her face as she understands she is late. Preserve look direction and plausible clock height.

d: Negative space in negative space cinematography leaves a large, relatively empty area around or beside the subject so absence becomes a mass. The unoccupied field is still a world (sky, wall, snow, sea), and the subject occupies a small or unusual portion of the diagram.
p: A young woman sits in the bottom-right corner of a tall, nearly empty waiting room. Most of the frame is pale wall and high windows. She looks toward the near edge rather than into the empty space. Static shot, restrained performance, no decorative camera movement.

d: One-point perspective in one point perspective cinematography squares the camera to a plane so receding parallels meet at a single vanishing point, often on the central axis. The result is tunnel depth or ceremonial order: a corridor, a nave, a hotel hall aimed at infinity or at a person.
p: A lone night porter stands centered at the end of a perfectly symmetrical hotel corridor. Locked axial camera, central vanishing point, balanced lamps and doorways. Hold still as one door on the far left opens slightly, breaking the order. No camera move.

d: Reflections in reflection cinematography put observer and observed in one plane by using glass, water, chrome, or a mirror. Mirror dialogue and one-way-glass staging let two spaces occupy a single composition, because optics, not a filter, do the doubling.
p: A man and woman speak across a one-way-glass booth. Her illuminated face is visible while his dim reflection gradually overlays the glass as the light balance changes. Keep their positions consistent and the reflection optically plausible. Slow, restrained performance; no supernatural double.

d: Repetition and pattern composition repeats shapes, colors, lines, positions, or actions so the eye reads a system of columns, windows, soldiers, or hotel doors. A break in that pattern is often the story, because the grid had already set the expectation.
p: Create two versions of a woman’s morning walk through the same apartment courtyard. First, she ignores three neighbors while checking her phone. Later, repeat the camera positions and route, but she greets each neighbor and notices a repaired fountain. Keep the environment consistent so changed attention, not a new location, carries the meaning.

d: The rule of thirds in rule of thirds cinematography divides the frame into nine equal cells and parks important masses on those lines or at their four intersections. The horizon usually sits on an upper or lower third so land and sky are not equal partners, and the subject usually sits off-center with look-space in the larger remaining field.
p: Rule-of-thirds placement of [Subject] on a power intersection, horizon on a third, breathing room in the look direction.

d: Screen in screen (desktop film, interface as the camera) nests a monitor, phone, television, or cinema inside the cinema so someone is watching a picture of someone. The inner image has its own crop, delay, and artifacts, and nested looking is the diagram.
p: Create a desktop-screen short: a woman starts writing an apology email, deletes it, receives an old photo and opens a video call she hesitates to answer. Generate the photo and call footage separately. Build the interface, readable text, cursor path and notification timing with code or compositing. No unreadable AI-generated UI text.

d: Short siding places the face near the frame edge the character looks toward, crushing look-space and leaving surplus air behind the head. The edge they face becomes a wall, so the diagram denies them a future in the picture.
p: Short-sided framing of [Subject], look space crushed, the face near the frame edge they look toward, trapped or urgent.

d: Symmetry in a symmetrical composition balances visual masses around an axis, usually the vertical centerline, so left answers right. The world looks designed, or it is pretending to be, whether or not a person occupies the middle.
p: Perfect symmetry around [Subject], mirrored architecture, a central axis, obsessive order.

d: A tableau (tableau vivant, frontal ensemble, or frieze) is a staged composition whose meaning develops inside a relatively fixed frame. Arranged bodies and objects form a living picture, so duration replaces coverage while the camera stays locked or nearly locked.
p: Locked wide frontal shot of five museum attendants preparing a display. Each performs a different small task; one repeatedly moves an object that another immediately returns. Clear spacing, readable full-body gestures, dry visual humor, no close-ups or camera motion.

d: Tonal contrast, the contrast composition of lightest against darkest mass, organizes the frame as a fight of value with the subject as one of those poles. Graphic punch replaces mid-grey mush, so the diagram reads as a poster of value rather than a gentle range of detail.
p: High tonal contrast composition with [Subject] as the lightest or darkest mass, graphic punch, no mid-gray mush.

d: Triangular composition arranges subjects or visual masses into a triangle so three points lock the frame. A group gets a hierarchy: the apex is usually power, witness, or the object of desire, and the base is support, threat, or the audience inside the picture.
p: Triangular arrangement with [Subject] at an apex, three masses locking the frame, Renaissance blocking.

d: A vanishing point in vanishing point composition is the apparent meeting place of parallel lines in perspective, a destination for rails, a road, or a colonnade. The person often stands as a gate in front of that meeting, or occupies it as the target of the architecture.
p: Deep vanishing point beyond [Subject], rails or road sucking the eye to infinity, the person as a gate.

d: Visual weight in visual weight composition is the attention an element attracts through size, contrast, color, position, focus, faces, or motion. A small bright thing can equal a large dark mass, because scale of attention is not scale of object.
p: Composition balancing visual weight around [Subject], a bright small thing equal to a large dark mass, scale of attention.

d: A void in void cinematography erases the set: darkness, white, or a blank field eating the world until a figure stands against nothing. Negative space still belongs to a place, while a void deletes place, leaving almost no landlord but the body or the darkness that might eat it.
p: Void around [Subject], darkness or blank field eating the world, a figure against nothing.

d: Voyeur cinematography places the camera in concealment so the audience is trespassing: a view through foliage, glass, a grate, or a distant window, often with dirty edges. The diagram is a peephole, not coverage, and the owner of that hide does not want us there.
p: Locked shot inside a dim railway waiting room. An unseen suitcase rolls across the platform outside; its wheels move audibly from left to right, pause, then return. The lone passenger reacts without the camera revealing the source. Design spatially coherent audio separately, with no visible creature or arbitrary musical sting.

d: Windows cinematography treats panes as the true subject: stacked apertures, lives in rectangles, a building of frames. The diagram is a grid of possible pictures, not one doorway around one face.
p: Windows as the true subject around [Subject], stacked apertures, lives in rectangles, a building of frames.

d: A 135mm telephoto in 135mm cinematography is a long lens used from a distant stand so planes stack and the background crowds the figure. The image feels like eavesdropping: you are far away, yet the world presses in.
p: 135mm telephoto on [Subject], stacked planes, eavesdropping compression, background crowding the figure.

d: A 14mm ultra-wide in 14mm cinematography is a very short focal length that, from a close stand, takes in a huge field and exaggerates near-to-far size. The close camera position, not the millimeter stamp alone, is what balloons a foreground face or object against a receding room.
p: Very close wide-angle portrait of a tired night cook leaning toward the camera in a tiny kitchen. His near hand appears larger, the room stretches strongly behind him, walls remain rigid. Expressive perspective, natural facial anatomy, no fisheye circle.

d: A 200mm long telephoto in 200mm cinematography is an extreme long lens used from a very distant stand so size differences between planes almost vanish. Heat shimmer, stacked terrain, and sniper intimacy are the physical leftovers of that throw.
p: 200mm long lens on [Subject], extreme compression, heat shimmer, isolated from a distance, sniper intimacy.

d: A 24mm wide in 24mm lens cinematography is a moderately wide prime that holds a person and a usable amount of place without extreme stretch. Body and architecture share the rectangle; neither fully wins.
p: 24mm wide on [Subject], environmental portrait, body in space, moderate stretch, reportage cinema.

d: A 35mm moderate wide in 35mm cinematography is the common narrative wide-normal: natural perspective with a little more world than a 50mm. It is default coverage for scenes that need both face and room.
p: 35mm on [Subject], the classic storyteller focal length, natural perspective with a little more world than 50.

d: A 50mm normal in 50mm cinematography is the conventional normal prime: from a typical stand it neither stretches near space nor stacks distant planes. The glass refuses to editorialize perspective; camera position still does all of that work.
p: 50mm normal lens on [Subject], human-eye perspective, neither compressed nor stretched, conversational truth.

d: An 85mm portrait in 85mm cinematography is a short telephoto used from a farther stand so a head-and-shoulders stays large while the background enlarges and recedes in importance. The person becomes the landscape; the room becomes stacked color and shape behind them.
p: 85mm portrait of [Subject], compressed background, beautiful falloff, isolation, the face as the only country.

d: Anamorphic cinematography squeezes one image dimension during capture, usually horizontally by 2x, then expands it for presentation. Depending on the lens, that cylindrical squeeze can produce oval bokeh, directional flares, and distinctive edge behavior; a wide aspect ratio alone is not anamorphic photography.
p: Night exterior of a woman beneath station lights, widescreen anamorphic-style optics, subtle oval defocused highlights and restrained horizontal flare from one practical light. Natural face width, coherent architecture, no excessive streaks and no letterbox bars baked into the image.

d: A fisheye in fisheye cinematography is a very wide curvilinear projection that bends straight lines, especially away from the center. The world wraps around the lens; architecture becomes a bowl rather than a rectilinear box.
p: A palace official stands small at the center of an enormous ornate chamber, filmed with a frame-filling fisheye look. Walls bow smoothly toward the edges, ceiling and floor remain structurally coherent. Slow restrained action, locked camera, no circular black border.

d: Macro cinematography is close-focusing optics that let a small object or surface occupy the image at high reproduction scale, often near 1:1. An unusually close view turns texture, insects, eyes, or mechanisms into the entire shot.
p: Extreme macro shot of a watchmaker lowering one tiny screw into an old brass mechanism. The screw head and adjacent gear teeth are crisp; focus falls away rapidly. One slow precise movement, realistic metal scale, no oversized fingers or morphing gears.

d: Magnification in magnification cinematography is the ratio of the subject's image size on the sensor to its real size. High magnification makes a centimeter of the world fill the frame; it is a scale number, not a shot-size name and not automatically a macro lens.
p: Extreme magnification of [Subject], a world inside a centimeter, scale lost on purpose.

d: A probe lens is a long, narrow macro optic that can pass through small spaces and create extreme close moving shots from inside the subject. The front element is tiny and far from the camera body, so the viewpoint can enter a glass, a wound of machinery, food, or a miniature set.
p: Probe-lens view of [Subject], tiny wide lens on a stick, impossible proximity through glass, food, or machinery, miniature world.

d: A spherical lens in spherical lens cinematography uses rotationally symmetric elements with no anamorphic squeeze, so the image is captured already in its display proportions. Bokeh from a round iris is round, and edges stay rectilinear aside from ordinary wide-angle stretch.
p: Spherical prime on [Subject], round bokeh, rectilinear edges, clean modern capture, no anamorphic streak.

d: A split diopter is a partial close-focus element that keeps different distance zones sharp in one frame. One region focuses very near while another remains focused farther away; it is not two focal lengths, and it is not ordinary deep focus.
p: A listening device fills the near-left foreground; a suspicious figure stands far back on the right. Both are tack sharp, with a narrow soft transition aligned to a dark door jamb between them. Locked camera, deliberate split-diopter look, not uniformly sharp depth throughout the room.
