d: Telephoto compression in lens compression cinematography is the perspective effect of a distant viewpoint: size differences between separated depth planes shrink, so a crowd or a city appears to press against a person. A long lens then frames that distant view tightly; a long lens from a close stand does not create the effect.
p: From far away with a long lens, frame one cyclist approaching along a straight road. Successive streetlights appear densely stacked behind him and his approach seems slow despite steady pedaling. Heat shimmer, fixed camera, no wide-angle expansion or zoom.

d: Tilt-shift cinematography tilts the lens relative to the sensor so the plane of focus rotates, and may also shift the lens to slide perspective. A narrow band or shaped region of sharpness, often from a high viewpoint, can make a real-scale scene resemble a small model.
p: High oblique view of two rowing teams moving along a river, with a narrow depth-aware focus region around the boats and smoothly increasing blur nearer and farther away. Slightly brisk motion and crisp miniature-like detail. No actual toy proportions, no arbitrary blurry stripe across faces.

d: Vintage cine glass is older motion-picture optics whose coatings, contrast, and aberrations differ from modern clinical primes. Lower contrast, gentle halation, and sometimes swirling or rolling edges are properties of the lens, not a grade slapped on sharp digital.
p: Vintage cine glass on [Subject], lower contrast, gentle halation, swirling edges, Cooke or K35 romance, not clinical sharpness.

d: Bleach bypass retains silver during processing, or simulates that retention, so the dye image sits on leftover metallic density. Contrast rises, grain shows, saturation falls, and highlights turn harsh rather than candy-colored.
p: Rain-soaked industrial street with restrained color, dense but separated blacks, pale stressed skin and hard wet highlights. Bleach-bypass-inspired tonal treatment, visible fine texture, no crushed black voids or monochrome conversion. Slow observational camera.

d: A color shift effect is a change of color state that the audience is meant to notice: monochrome to hue, one world to another, or a slide of temperature during the shot. Color is the event, not a hidden LUT.
p: Inside a muted sepia workshop, a child opens a large door onto a richly colored greenhouse. Keep the interior sepia while the exterior already exists in color beyond the threshold. As the camera crosses the doorway, enter the full-color world. No dissolve or global color wash.

d: A cool blue grade in cool color grade work shifts the image toward steel, cyan, or moonlight blues across shadows and often midtones. Warmth, if it survives, is reserved for a practical or a face that the story wants to save.
p: Cool blue grade on [Subject], steel shadows, hospital or moonlight, warmth reserved for one practical if any.

d: A cross process look imitates developing a film in the wrong chemistry, such as slide stock in color-negative developer, so primaries skew off their true identities. Contrast often climbs; cyan shadows, magenta or yellow skin shifts, and other chemical accidents become the palette.
p: Cross-processed look on [Subject], skewed primaries, cyan shadows, magenta skin shift, music-video chemical accident.

d: Day for night cinematography photographs daylight so it will read as nighttime while still showing terrain that true night might hide. Exposure, sky, and highlight control do the lying; a blue wash alone is not the technique.
p: A wide horse ranch under apparent moonlight: deep dark sky, subtly readable distant hills, muted color and believable cool low-level illumination. One rider crosses the field. No bright daytime clouds, no obvious noon shadows, no uniform blue overlay. Generate a controlled base and grade sky and terrain separately.

d: Desaturation in desaturated cinematography reduces color intensity while leaving hue present. The world is wintered or dusted; leftover accents still speak, but chroma is no longer loud.
p: Desaturated palette on [Subject], chroma pulled back, dusty, wintered, emotion in leftover color accents.

d: A filmic faded grade in filmic color grade work imitates a print: blacks are lifted off true zero, highlights roll off instead of clipping like video, and contrast sits like photochemical display. It is not HDR punch, and it is not automatically period costume.
p: Filmic faded grade on [Subject], lifted blacks, rolled-off highlights, print-emulation, slightly expired romance.

d: Hyper-saturation in saturated cinematography raises color intensity past ordinary record, so hues read as lacquer, fever, or dream. Feeling is louder than fact; the palette is not documentary.
p: Hyper-saturated color on [Subject], Velvia intensity, reds like lacquer, a dream or a fever, not documentary.

d: Monochrome, including black and white cinematography, removes or does not record chromatic information so the image is value, texture, and shape. Hue is gone; contrast, grain, and outline do the talking.
p: Monochrome treatment of [Subject], silver highlights, deep blacks, no chroma, shape and light only.

d: Moonlight gel in moonlight lighting gel work is a cool, often cyan or steel-green key standing in for the moon, usually a large source from above or through trees. Night stays sculpted: there is a direction, a rim, and deep underexposure, not only a blue grade.
p: A dancer crosses an empty rehearsal room divided between deep crimson side light and cold cobalt light from the opposite side. Colors remain spatially separate and shift across her body as she moves. Rich blacks, deliberate theatrical unreality, no rainbow lighting or pulsing nightclub effects.

d: A natural color grade keeps skin faithful and saturation restrained so the location's real color science remains the authority. No stylized split, no silver punishment, no fever: the grade mostly refuses to editorialize hue.
p: Natural grade on [Subject], faithful skin, restrained saturation, no stylized split, the location

d: Overexposed cinematography lets values clip or bloom toward white on purpose so information in the highlights is burned. It is a choice to lose the top of the scale, not the same as high-key lighting, which can stay bright while still holding detail.
p: Overexposed [Subject], values clipping toward heaven or fluorescent hell, information burned on purpose.

d: A color palette in color palette cinematography is a restricted set of hues used as law across set, costume, light, and grade. Too many colors would be noise; a few chosen hues do all the work and can mark location, timeline, or story state.
p: Generate three matched views of one train-station meeting as alternate recollections: warm amber, cool blue-gray and restrained white-green. Keep blocking and character identities identical while wardrobe accents, environment and light follow each version’s palette. Assemble as distinct narrative strands rather than cycling hues within one shot.

d: Sepia tone in sepia tone film maps the grey scale onto brown-gold instead of neutral silver, so whites go toward faded paper and blacks toward umber. It is a color of the past as chemistry, not a warm grade on a full-hue world.
p: Sepia tonality on [Subject], brown-gold memory, faded whites, the past as a color, not a filter sticker.

d: Split toning in split toning cinematography assigns one hue to highlights and another to shadows, so the tone curve becomes a two-color world. Any pair is legal; teal-and-orange is only one famous instance.
p: Split-toned grade on [Subject], highlights one hue, shadows another, for example gold over teal, a two-color world.

d: A teal and orange color grade pushes shadows and often skies toward cyan-teal while keeping skin and warm sources in the orange half of the wheel. It is a complementary split with faces protected, not a silver-retention process and not a general cool wash.
p: Teal-and-orange grade on [Subject], skin staying warm, shadows and skies pushed cyan, blockbuster complementary split.

d: Tungsten balance in tungsten color temperature work sets the camera or stock for about 3200K so tungsten practicals render near-neutral or gently warm while daylight and cooler sources go blue. Different source colors remain visibly distinct rather than being normalized to one white.
p: A woman sits at a kitchen table lit by a warm tungsten pendant while cold blue predawn light enters from a window behind her. Both colors stay distinct, natural skin transitions, readable shadows. She turns toward the window and moves from warmth into cooler light.

d: A vintage film look treats the image as past chemistry: faded dyes, possible halation, softened contrast, and period color that has drifted. It is a whole-file costume of time, not only old glass and not only a lifted print curve.
p: Vintage treatment of [Subject], faded dyes, halation, the past as chemistry, not a sticker.

d: A warm amber grade in warm color grade work biases mids and highlights toward tungsten honey, candle, and practical glow. Safety, home, or nostalgia sits in the mids; the world is invited rather than chilled.
p: Warm amber grade on [Subject], tungsten honey, candle and practical glow, safety or nostalgia in the mids.

d: A boomerang video effect plays a short action forward, then snaps it backward along the same samples, often looping. The gesture comes and goes on one path: reversed playback used as a round trip rather than a one-way undo.
p: [Subject] plays forward then reverses along the same motion, a seamless boomerang loop.

d: Bullet time freezes or radically slows action while the viewpoint travels around it, decoupling camera speed from subject time. The instant becomes inspectable space: a time-slice orbit around a sculpture of speed, not ordinary slow motion with a handheld camera.
p: A dancer is suspended at the peak of a leap while loose paper hangs around her. The camera moves smoothly through a 90-degree arc at normal viewing speed while the leap advances only slightly. Consistent anatomy, rigid paper shapes, coherent shadows, no repeated body limbs. Build with multi-view keyframes or 3D for control.

d: Fast motion cinematography compresses screen duration so action plays faster than it occurred, by undercranking the camera or by retiming a normal-rate take. Crowds smear, clouds race, and labor can look absurdly efficient because too many events occupy too little time.
p: A harried mailroom worker sorts envelopes in slightly accelerated motion while maintaining physically coherent hand actions. Fixed medium-wide view, increasingly comic efficiency, no teleporting objects or time-lapse crowd trails. Retime a clean base shot if exact cadence is required.

d: A freeze frame holds one image so narrative time stops while camera, subject, and world all cease to generate new samples. The hold can end a story, land a joke, or present a face as evidence.
p: Edit a group of exhausted friends leaving an all-night diner at sunrise to an original energetic rock cue. Let the first strong beat land on the door opening, then allow the song to continue over several distinct street moments. Use a newly composed track, not a replica of an existing film song.

d: Frozen in motion stops the environment and most people while a chosen character, the viewpoint, or both continue to move. Particles, extras, and pigeons hang, and the rule of who may move is the entire effect.
p: A woman walks through a city square where all other people are motionless mid-gesture and pigeons hang in the air. Only she, her clothing and the following camera move. Coherent suspended poses, no breathing crowds, no melting birds, quiet suspended mood.

d: An infinite loop video sews the last frame to the first so motion never arrives at an ending. The cycle can be a seamless visual join, or, in narrative use, a repeated day whose variables change.
p: Design three repetitions of a commuter’s morning: the same alarm, dropped coin and departing bus. In each cycle she changes one decision, producing a different encounter. Reuse matched camera positions and reset sounds. Generate the baseline once, then controlled variations with stable people and geography.

d: Long take cinematography is an unusually extended shot that preserves continuous performance, space, action, or duration without an overt cut. Blocking and camera share one sentence so the audience cannot leave the room.
p: Follow a harbor nurse through an improvised waiting area after a storm. In one flowing shot, pass people playing cards, repairing a radio, tending injuries and staring silently at the sea. No disaster spectacle; distinct actions continue independently in depth. Keep the nurse as a loose visual anchor.

d: Low shutter cinematography uses a short shutter angle or short exposure so moving edges stay sharp inside each frame. Normal-rate action then feels abrupt and staccato because this is reduced motion blur, not a long-exposure smear.
p: Handheld close action of a rescue crew running through heavy rain, normal playback speed but crisp short-exposure droplets and sharply segmented body movement. Readable geography, restrained shake, no smooth slow motion, no artificial frame skipping.

d: A moonwalk effect is a backward glide that reads as a forward myth: the torso stays upright, one foot slides, the other pushes, and the heel does not lift like a walk. It is a locomotion lie in living time, not reversed footage.
p: [Subject] glides backward as if the floor were ice, a moonwalk path.

d: Motion blur cinematography is the streaking or softness caused by subject or camera movement during exposure. The longer the gate stays open relative to the motion, the more the image paints, so edges fail on purpose.
p: Heavy motion blur as [Subject] or the camera moves, light streaking, shutter dragged.

d: A oner shot is designed to play as if the scene were one take, with no visible edits. It may be a true single take or a stitched oner whose joins hide in whips, darkness, or crossing bodies.
p: A continuous oner following [Subject] through connected actions without a visible cut.

d: Reverse motion plays recorded action backward so causes arrive after their effects inside the shot: rain rises, smoke inhales, a shattered object reassembles. This is reversed playback, not a story told in reverse scene order.
p: Create four ordinary-speed scenes about a broken friendship: an unopened apology, a public argument, a misunderstood message and an earlier act of trust. Present them in reverse chronological order. At each transition, reveal a cause that changes the previous scene’s meaning. Do not run the footage backward.

d: Slow motion cinematography plays action over more screen time than the event occupied during capture, usually by overcranking (recording 120 to 240 fps and playing at 24). The extra samples reveal fabric delay, particle hang, and impact mechanics that a 24 fps shutter would compress into a few smeared frames.
p: A glass slips from a waiter’s hand and falls in elegant slow motion. Fingers release naturally, the glass rotates coherently and fabric moves with plausible inertia. Locked close shot, smooth temporal detail, no frozen background or bullet-time orbit.

d: Speed ramping changes playback or capture speed inside a single shot rather than holding one retiming ratio. Approach and recovery stay energetic while one motivated instant (impact, glance, turn) stretches, then the clock returns.
p: A skateboarder approaches a small ramp at normal speed, slows smoothly to reveal the board rotating beneath their feet, then returns to normal speed on landing. One coherent action, readable foot placement, natural gravity, no impossible extra spin. Specify and refine the ramp in editing.

d: Step printing repeats or omits frames optically or digitally so motion advances in visible temporal steps. Combined with low-rate capture and long exposures, each frame smears internally while the sequence stutters forward, a texture of delay rather than clean high-frame-rate slow motion.
p: A lonely man stands at a night food counter while pedestrians stream past as smeared, stuttering shapes. His small movements remain readable. Long-exposure motion texture with deliberate repeated-frame cadence, saturated practical lights, no clean high-frame-rate slow motion. Apply the cadence in post from a controlled base clip.

d: Stop motion cinematography photographs physical objects incrementally, adjusting them between exposures so successive poses create apparent movement. The cadence is pose to pose and slightly staccato, with tactile materials in the light.
p: An articulated paper-and-wire fox carefully folds a paper boat on a miniature desk. Tactile materials, consistent joint construction, deliberate frame-by-frame posing and small controlled increments. Stable lighting and set, readable hand-object contact, no fluid live-action fur or continuously melting paper.

d: Stutter editing drops or repeats frames so playback skips and the world's clock hitches. It is an anxious rhythm, not the lyric smear of step printing and not a jump cut's spatial jump.
p: Stuttering playback of [Subject], frames repeating and skipping, anxious rhythm.

d: Time-lapse cinematography captures frames at long intervals so slow change plays as continuous motion, hours becoming seconds as shadows sweep and crowds become flow. It is interval photography, not a sped-up ordinary take.
p: Locked high view of a public square from early morning to night, compressed into ten seconds. Shadows move continuously, crowds form and dissolve, windows light up gradually. Stable buildings and weather logic, no morphing architecture. Generate controlled day-phase keyframes and assemble a time-lapse progression.

d: Timelapse glam is interval photography of a styling process in which clothes, hair, and makeup change at high speed while the face holds. The person is a still axis and wardrobe is the changing weather.
p: Time-lapse around a still [Subject] as stylists and wardrobe change at high speed.

d: Timelapse human holds one person in living time while the crowd is interval-sampled into smoke, so one still will stands in a rushing system. It is the opposite clock of a frozen world with a moving hero.
p: Crowds time-lapse around a still [Subject], the city racing, the person holding.

d: Timelapse landscape interval-samples light and weather over a place so hours play in seconds as clouds and shadows sweep. Geography is the actor, and a person, if present, is a scale mark rather than a racing extra.
p: Time-lapse of light and weather over the landscape of [Subject].

d: Altered state cinematography makes the mind the location: smear, afterimage, wrong color, unstable time, optics and cutting that no sober observer would report. It is a bundle of techniques motivated by consciousness, not a single filter name.
p: The frame around [Subject] warps as if consciousness is slipping, edges trailing, color unhooked from the room.

d: An anamorphic flare is a horizontal streak produced when a bright point hits the cylindrical elements of an anamorphic lens. It is a subset of lens flare, not a general haze, and it usually arrives with oval bokeh from the same squeeze.
p: Horizontal anamorphic flares streaking through [Subject], cyan or magenta bars, oval bokeh, scope cinema signature.

d: Anthropomorphic cinematography stages an object or animal as a performer: human scale in the frame, a gesture, an eyeline, reaction shots, as if the inanimate had a will. The camera does not need a face so much as an actor's grammar.
p: Anthropomorphic frame of [Subject], an object or animal given human scale, gesture, or eyeline, the inanimate performing.

d: An Argus image, argus many eyes, fills the frame with looking: extra pupils on a body, a swarm of viewpoints, a creature or a city of eyes. The surplus is seeing, counted as organs or cameras, not as flare.
p: Argus image of [Subject], many eyes, many viewpoints, a creature or a city of looking.

d: Bokeh in bokeh cinematography is the aesthetic character of out-of-focus rendering: the disc shape, edge, and smoothness of blurred points, not the mere fact of a thin depth of field. The glass, not a blur slider, decides whether those discs are round, oval, outlined, or swirling.
p: Creamy bokeh field behind [Subject], circular or oval highlights, the world melted to light, subject isolated by glass.

d: Bubbles cinematography fills the air with little lenses: soap films that refract the subject, rainbow edges, wet highlights. Each bubble is an optic, not a disk of bokeh.
p: Bubbles around [Subject], refraction worlds, cheap magic that still reads as joy or threat.

d: Chromatic aberration in chromatic aberration cinematography is color fringing from different wavelengths focusing at different distances or magnifications. Lateral CA puts red-cyan (or similar) fringes on high-contrast edges, worse toward the frame edge, while longitudinal CA puts different colors in front of and behind the focus plane.
p: Chromatic aberration on [Subject], red-cyan fringing at high-contrast edges, cheap glass or dream distortion.

d: A cinemagraph is a still photograph in which one isolated element continues to move on a loop (steam, rain on glass, hair, a blink) while the rest of the frame is frozen. It is not a freeze-frame of a whole shot, and it is not a full clip that happens to loop.
p: Almost still on [Subject], only one element loops: steam, rain, or a subtle gesture.

d: Collage cinematography builds a frame from torn, cut, or mixed pieces: different stocks, paper, print, and live action sharing one plane with visible joins. Edges are graphic, and the stack is a construction, not an optical blend.
p: Collage frame of [Subject], torn layers, mixed stocks, cut paper and live action sharing one plane.

d: A cyclope camera is one giant iris looking: fisheye as a monster eye, a single hole, too close. The lens is the creature.
p: Cyclope view of [Subject], a single giant iris, fisheye as a monster eye, one hole looking.

d: Datamosh is intentional codec failure: inter-frame prediction continues after keyframes are removed or broken, so motion vectors smear the previous picture into the next GOP and faces bleed into the following shot. The image is file wreckage, not a lens error.
p: Datamosh corruption around [Subject], frames bleeding into the next, codec wreckage as image.

d: Deep focus in deep focus cinematography keeps multiple near and far planes legibly sharp in one image. It is a continuous depth of field, not merely action arranged in depth while the glass stays selective.
p: Locked wide shot of a courthouse office: a clerk’s hand stamps a form near the lens while an anxious visitor stands in a distant doorway. Both near and far action remain sharply readable, natural perspective, no rack focus, no artificial split-screen seam.

d: Diorama cinematography photographs a physical scale model so that it stands in for a much larger object or environment, with real light hitting real miniature surfaces. Scale is sold by texture, camera speed, depth of field, and movement, not by a toy-like tilt of focus.
p: Photograph a practical-looking miniature orbital freighter as if it were enormous. Slow precise camera pass, deep enough focus for convincing scale, hard distant key light, tiny windows and layered surface detail. No shallow tabletop focus or fast toy-like acceleration.

d: Lens distortion cinematography warps space so straight lines bow, stretch, or melt: barrel, pincushion, mustache, extreme wide stretch, or a physical distorting optic such as a diopter, a bottle, or rain on glass. The lens is lying about geometry, not adding flare.
p: Optical distortion around [Subject], stretched edges, melted geometry, the lens lying about space.

d: Double exposure in double exposure film combines two or more image records on one frame, in camera by winding back, optically in a printer, or digitally as an additive composite. Both pictures occupy the same emulsion or file unless a matte fully holds one off.
p: A woman argues with an identical version of herself across a kitchen table. Generate each performance as a separate plate from the same locked camera and clean kitchen reference. Match eyelines and timing; keep their silhouettes separate. Composite them together with consistent shadows and no identity blending.

d: A duplicate subject effect puts the same performer in a frame more than once as solid bodies: twins, a self across a table, copies in one room. It is usually a split matte, motion control, or a locked-camera composite, not a translucent double exposure.
p: Duplication of [Subject], the same figure twice or more in one frame, twins of time or identity.

d: An echo print is an echo print effect that leaves a ghosted afterimage offset in time or register, so the last pose is still printed on this frame. The ghost is a stain of a previous exposure, not a second complete picture sharing the same plane.
p: Afterimages of [Subject] trail the present, an echo print of the previous moment.

d: Video feedback is made by pointing a camera at its own live output so the picture nests into a recursive corridor of the same face. Each generation is a rephotograph of the monitor, with bloom, lag, and a tunnel of shrinking frames.
p: Recursive video feedback of [Subject], the image eating itself into a tunnel.

d: Film grain in film grain cinematography is the random texture of silver halide crystals or color dye clouds in the emulsion, or a digital simulation of that structure. It is a developed surface, not a PNG overlay sitting on top of a clean render.
p: Visible film grain over [Subject], 35mm or 16mm texture, living silver, not a cheap overlay.

d: A floating fall is a body hanging in a slow drop: delayed gravity on hair and coat, still going down. The path remains toward the ground, even when the clock on the body is late.
p: [Subject] falls in slow, floating pieces, delayed gravity, a dream of dropping.

d: Floating UI, or HUD overlay cinematography, places readable interface, callouts, and data planes in the air of the scene so information lives in space, not only on a physical screen. The cockpit is the room.
p: Floating UI over [Subject], HUD, callouts, and interface planes in 3D space, the screen as a cockpit.

d: A focal shift moves the plane of sharpness from one subject or distance to another during the shot, so attention travels as a pull. The camera body can stay put, and only the focus mechanism walks the depth.
p: Focus pulls from a foreground object onto [Subject], or the reverse.

d: Focus change cinematography jumps or slides the plane of sharpness to a new fact, a rack without apology. The mid-blur is short, and the new plane owns the shot as soon as it lands.
p: Focus changes from one plane onto [Subject] or away from them.

d: Forced perspective uses camera position, subject distance, and set geometry to alter apparent size or distance, and the lie exists only from the taking viewpoint. Bodies, furniture, and eyelines must agree or the scale collapses.
p: From one locked camera, a tiny adult guest sits beside a normal-sized host at a rustic table. Design the table and seating in separate scaled sections so their eyelines meet correctly. Stable hands, feet and contact shadows; no shrinking animation or distorted anatomy.

d: Generative visuals show process: forms grown by rule, particles, and iteration, so cinema is made by a system rather than only by a finished photograph. Making is visible.
p: Generative image of [Subject], forms grown by rule, particles, and iteration, cinema made by a system.

d: Halation in film is a reddish or warm glow around bright highlights caused by light passing through the emulsion, reflecting off the base, and scattering back into the image. It is a stock behavior, not a diffusion filter and not flare inside the lens.
p: A woman reads beside a bright summer window. Fine facial detail stays readable while window highlights bloom gently into the surrounding air. Subtle soft filtration, luminous skin without smoothing away texture, no fog overlay or global defocus.

d: Infrared cinematography photographs near-infrared reflectance (roughly 700 to 900 nm), not heat, so foliage often goes pale, skies go dark, and skin can look waxy. It is a different slice of reflected light, still a photograph of the location.
p: Infrared look on [Subject], foliage going pale, skies black, skin otherworldly, a spectrum humans do not own.

d: Kaleidoscope cinematography fragments the image with mirrors or radial repetition so one subject becomes a symmetric pattern. The camera looks into angled glass, or the staging itself is a kaleidoscope: bodies arranged around an axis, often from above.
p: Kaleidoscopic fragmentation of [Subject], mirrored shards, Busby Berkeley from inside a jewel.

d: Lens flare in lens flare cinematography is stray light scattered by glass, coatings, and barrel walls, producing ghosts, streaks, or veiling glare instead of a clean image. The artifacts live in the taking optic, so they track the source angle and dim when a body occludes the lamp.
p: A rescue worker opens a hangar door onto dazzling daylight. As the source enters the lens angle, a restrained flare and brief veiling glare wash across the image, then clear as she blocks it. Realistic source-linked behavior, no floating decorative rainbow effects.

d: A levitation shot holds a body or object in a quiet impossible hover, refusing ordinary gravity while support is hidden or removed. Hair and cloth still hang, and the gap under the feet is the proof.
p: A fictional acrobat crosses between two low rooftops in one graceful extended leap. Clear push-off, smooth rising arc, brief suspension and weighted landing with knees absorbing impact. Loose fabric follows the body with delay. Fixed wide camera, consistent architecture, no teleportation or rubber limbs.

d: A light flash transition is a brief blowout of the frame to white or near-white, then a return, as if a bulb, explosion, or memory dump hit the emulsion. It is a temporal event, often a cut hidden in the peak, not a standing lens flare.
p: A hard light flash blows out [Subject] then settles back, as a memory or explosion sting.

d: A light leak in light leak film is unfiltered light that reaches the emulsion or sensor without passing through the taking lens, usually through a gap in the body, magazine, or gate. It fogs from the edge or along a scratch in the film path, often orange or red on color negative because it hits the base side.
p: Analog light leak washing [Subject], orange or red flare eating the frame edge, a wound in the emulsion.

d: Masking cinematography uses a matte, a viewfinder object, or a graphic window so looking is visible as a shape cutting the picture. We see through binoculars, a keyhole, or a hard-edged hole.
p: Masked frame around [Subject], a shape cutting the picture, binoculars, a keyhole, a graphic window.

d: Mixed media film combines live action with type, illustration, and stock in one plane so no single capture method owns the truth of the frame. Media collide rather than dissolve into one photograph.
p: Mixed media around [Subject], live action, type, illustration, and stock colliding in one plane.

d: A morphing effect transforms one image, face, shape, or object into another by interpolating corresponding geometry over time. It is a continuous becoming, not a crossfade of opacities and not two exposures stacked.
p: [Subject] morphs into another form or face over 6 seconds, a continuous transformation.

d: Morphing cinematography transforms one shape or image continuously into another by interpolating geometry, rather than merely fading between pictures. Identity is a dissolve you can watch as contour.
p: Transform a close-up of a young fictional woman’s face into her older self over four seconds. Keep eyes aligned, head pose, expression and light direction fixed. Age changes occur gradually and coherently. Use matched endpoint portraits and controlled landmark-based compositing, no identity swap or liquefying face.

d: Night vision in night vision cinematography is image intensification: residual photons, and often a near-IR illuminator, amplified through a photocathode and microchannel plate onto a phosphor. The picture is typically green, grainy, blooming around lamps, with the framing of goggles, a weapon sight, or a camera in the dark.
p: Night-vision green phosphor of [Subject], grainy, surveillance, found-footage military eye.

d: An object portal effect treats a prop as a wormhole: a bag, a screen, or a doorway that should not lead there, opening onto another space. The thing is the cut.
p: Object portal through [Subject], a thing opening onto another space, a bag, a screen, a doorway that should not lead there.

d: Particle effects cinematography fills the air with countable bits: dust, sparks, pollen, a weather of motes, each one catching light. Atmosphere you can inventory, not a blanket of fog.
p: Particles around [Subject], dust, sparks, pollen, a weather of bits, light catching each one.

d: The photogrammetry look reconstructs 3D geometry and texture from overlapping photographs, so a real place is turned into a scanned mesh. Slightly wrong normals, stretched texture, and holes are the evidence of capture.
p: Create a visualization concept for a spinning black hole with an accretion disk appearing lensed around the dark central region. Use a validated ray-traced simulation as the geometric reference and preserve its major contours. Label this as a cinematic visualization, not a newly computed scientific result.

d: Projections in projection mapping film put a pictured image onto a surface that the taking camera then photographs: front projection onto a retroreflective screen, rear projection behind a window or windshield, or video mapped onto architecture. The projector is a light source, and the set is also a screen.
p: A small practical-looking rocky foreground merges into an immense still desert panorama. Locked wide camera, performers lit to match the horizon photograph, subtle boundary between physical foreground and distant projected landscape. No drifting mountain geometry or independently moving horizon.

d: A rack focus moves the sharp plane from one subject or distance to another during a continuous shot, while the composition stays largely the same. Attention changes because the helical turns, not because the camera cuts or dollies.
p: Locked composition: a brass key in sharp foreground on a desk, a woman blurred in the doorway behind it. Hold the key, then slowly rack focus to her expression as the key becomes soft. No camera move, no zoom, neither object changes position.

d: An aspect ratio switch changes the image's visible boundaries so the container itself widens or closes as the story changes register. The picture is not stretched: previously unseen area is revealed, or the crop tightens.
p: Begin with a young cyclist confined within a square image. As she reaches an open seaside road and takes a deep breath, widen the frame smoothly to a broad rectangle, revealing the ocean on both sides. Reveal previously unseen image area; never stretch her body or bicycle. Animate the framing in post.

d: Scale shift cinematography changes a body's size against the same room so the figure is suddenly giant or tiny: Alice physics as an optical event. Furniture, shadows, and contact have to match the new ratio.
p: Design an intercut rescue story: a mountain team’s six-hour ascent, a driver’s thirty-minute approach and a climber’s final two-minute wait. Build a timeline showing exactly where they converge. Generate separate location strands and edit them toward one shared radio call, not as falsely equal real-time durations.

d: A selfie twin puts two of the same face in a phone-arm frame, identity as a double take at arm's length. The camera is a compact wide in a hand, not a hidden studio body.
p: Selfie twin of [Subject], two of the same face in a phone-arm frame, identity as a double take.

d: Shadow-box cinematography tells the story in layered cut-outs, depth as stacked silhouettes, a diorama of darkness. Figures are unfilled, and distance is paper stacked in front of a hard backlight.
p: Shadow-box of [Subject], layered cut-outs, depth as stacked silhouettes, a diorama of darkness.

d: Shallow focus keeps a narrow depth range sharp while foreground or background falls off. It is a depth-of-field choice made with distance, focal length, and aperture together, not a button labeled blur.
p: An elderly ticket seller sits behind glass in a busy station. Tight portrait with the near eye sharp and the crowd reduced to soft, unrecognizable shapes. Tiny natural movements, stable eye focus, no plastic skin, no abrupt background replacement.

d: Slit-scan exposes moving artwork or a moving camera through a narrow slit over time, stretching space into streaks and corridors with time laid along one axis. The result is structured geometry, not a random particle tunnel.
p: A sustained voyage through abstract planes of luminous geometry. Long parallel light streaks converge toward a stable central vanishing point, evolving through layered spatial corridors. Procedural slit-scan character, controlled acceleration, no literal starfield, random sparks or kaleidoscope cuts.

d: Smash-and-grab video is impact as coverage: glass, snatch, handheld chaos, a theft of a moment. The camera is inside the crime, too close and too late.
p: Violent handheld smash around [Subject], impact, grab, escape.

d: A sticker peel effect lifts the image from a backing: adhesive shine, a die-cut layer coming off the world. Thickness, curl, and glue are the physics, not a still collage of torn paper.
p: A sticker layer peels off [Subject] or the frame, revealing another layer.

d: Thermal imaging cinematography maps emitted long-wave infrared (heat), not reflected light. A microbolometer or similar sensor assigns a palette (white-hot, black-hot, ironbow) to temperature, so faces, engines, and blood read warm while cold metal and night air do not.
p: Thermal palette of [Subject], heat as color, faces as warm masks, Predator vision or search-and-rescue.

d: Transformation cinematography makes a body, room, or object become something else in continuous view. The camera keeps watching while the state changes, with a stable anchor so the becoming can be read.
p: Orbit slowly around two fictional former friends embracing in a modern station. Keep their bodies and contact continuous while the architecture behind them gradually becomes the childhood railway platform they remember. Change only the surrounding world, with coherent light and perspective. Plan matched environment plates and composite the transition; no melting faces.

d: Kinetic typography puts words in the world of the shot as objects: titles that occupy space, letters with scale, parallax, and a surface. The sentence is in the picture, not parked as a caption.
p: Design a forty-second title sequence for a film about a missing cartographer. A single ink line becomes a street, a fingerprint ridge and a coastline before vanishing at the edge of a map. Generate visual elements separately; animate the transformations and add exact credits in a motion-graphics timeline. No arbitrary stock-footage montage.

d: A vignette in vignette cinematography darkens, desaturates, or lowers contrast toward the frame edges because of optical falloff, mechanical vignetting in the barrel, a filter, or a later grade. Optical vignette follows the lens, while a post oval is a drawing.
p: Natural optical vignette around [Subject], edges falling off, attention pooled in the center, vintage falloff not a post oval.

d: A wigglegram is a short stereo shiver: two or three frames rocking so depth reads as a fidget. The viewpoints are a few centimeters apart, so depth is a twitch, not a dolly.
p: A short wiggle between two viewpoints of [Subject], stereoscopic shiver.

d: X-ray cinematography images through a surface as if denser structure were visible: bones, wiring, a body as diagram. Transmission, not reflectance, is the physics.
p: X-ray view of [Subject], interior structure, bones or wiring, a body as diagram.

d: Zoetrope cinematography shows the frames inside a movement: stroboscopic slices of a spinning action, motion as a drum of poses. You see the sampling, not a smooth blur.
p: Stroboscopic zoetrope slices of [Subject] in repeating action.

d: An axial cut jumps closer or farther along approximately the same camera axis, changing shot size without changing angle. The outgoing frame and the incoming frame share a viewpoint; only distance snaps.
p: A librarian notices an impossible new date stamped inside an old book. Make three hard cuts on the same axis: desk-wide, book close-up, extreme close-up of the date. Keep the page and hands fixed, with no zoom animation, morph or lateral angle change. Add exact date text in compositing.

d: A crash cut slams two images together with no blend, so the join itself stings. One side of the splice and the other collide; unlike a smash that breaks an earned quiet, a crash cut often starts inside the event or hits like a drum from the first frame.
p: Design three sequences: begin with a violinist standing alone on a flooded stage holding an unopened letter; cut to a calm morning before the concert; later return to the stage with the meaning of the letter now clear. Generate each sequence separately and edit the order deliberately. No unrelated mystery props.

d: Cross-cutting alternates two or more locations or action lines, often implying they are happening at the same time. Each side of the join is a complete strand; the engine is meanwhile, two clocks racing.
p: Generate A: a team approaches a building and presses a doorbell. Generate B: someone in a similar interior hears a bell and walks toward a door. Intercut as though they connect. Reveal in a wide reverse that B opens to a lone courier at a different address. Keep the earlier shots ambiguous rather than contradictory.

d: A dissolve gradually overlaps the outgoing shot with the incoming shot so both images occupy the frame for a measurable duration. Opacity of A falls as opacity of B rises; at the midpoint you are looking at two ghosts.
p: End on an old projector turning in a dark room. Let its rhythmic mechanical chatter continue across a cut to a sewing workshop, then resolve naturally into the sewing machine now on screen. Generate both pictures separately and match the two sound rhythms without a decorative visual dissolve.

d: A fade in or fade out takes the picture to or from a uniform field of black or color, rather than handing the frame straight to another visible scene. One side of the join is a world; the other side is absence, sleep, death, or a chapter break.
p: A woman closes her eyes in a quiet room. Fade the image slowly into deep dark red while the room’s ticking continues for one second, then stops. Hold the empty color field before the next scene. Produce the fade and sound timing in post, not as red smoke filling the room.

d: A flash cut interrupts the present image with a few frames of another picture, then returns or races on before the insert can be studied. One side of the join is the ongoing scene; the other is lightning: a thought, a future, a wound, lasting a blink.
p: Show brief intimate images of a woman teaching a child to repair a radio, initially without dates or age labels. In the present, she has never met the child. A later encounter reveals these are future moments. Generate stable radio and room details that make the temporal recognition precise.

d: Fragments, or fragmented editing, build an event from partial views, so the audience infers an action more complete than anything shown in one shot. Each side of a join is a shard: a blade, a mouth, a drain, a hand too late; the whole lives in the gaps.
p: Imply a valuable vase being accidentally knocked over without showing the full break. Generate separate shots of a sleeve brushing its base, a hand reaching too late, a startled face and ceramic pieces already on the floor. Join with one offscreen crash. No real hazardous stunt or incoherent object duplication.

d: A graphic match cut joins two images that share a dominant shape, line, color, placement, or motion pattern, even when location and time change. The outgoing contour and the incoming contour occupy the same part of the screen, so form carries you across the splice.
p: Generate A: close-up of a circular watch face centered in frame. Generate B: a circular observatory dome seen from above at exactly the same size and position. Hard-cut on the shared circle, with no morph or dissolve. Keep the two objects distinct and the visual connection immediate.

d: An invisible cut hides an edit through motion, darkness, occlusion, blur, matching geometry, or digital stitching. One side of the join and the other are meant to feel like a single take; the splice is a seam the audience should not find.
p: A stage magician drops a cloth over an empty chair. At the instant the cloth fills the chair silhouette, cut to an identically framed plate with a bouquet beneath it. The magician lifts the cloth. Locked camera, matching hands and shadows, no liquid morph or camera move. Generate two plates and join them at the occlusion.

d: An iris transition reveals or conceals the picture with a moving circular or shaped mask. The mask's center is a pointer: one side of the join is the full world, the other is a hole closing on a face, a detail, or black.
p: A violinist finishes a performance in an otherwise empty hall. Close a circular iris around her satisfied face, then let the circle reveal a tiny yawning cat on the piano before closing to black. Generate the clean scene and animate the mask separately.

d: A J-cut or L-cut visual setup is a picture designed so sound can lead or lag across the splice. One side of the join is a face, a room, or a listener that can hold; the other side is a space already speaking, or still speaking after we have left it.
p: A cheerful original corporate jingle plays over a spotless office being emptied after a sudden closure. Workers quietly pack plants and family photographs while the tune maintains its bright tempo. Generate restrained visual coverage and compose an original cue; do not imitate an existing recording or melody.

d: A jump cut removes time or slightly shifts framing inside a similar setup, so the discontinuity is conspicuous. The outgoing frame and the incoming frame are close enough that the missing interval reads as a skip, not as a new shot.
p: Locked medium shot of a woman waiting at a station bench. Make six jump cuts in the same framing as she changes posture, checks the clock and shifts her bag. Other passengers change between cuts. Clear elapsed waiting time, no morphing transitions or camera repositioning.

d: A match cut joins two shots through a visual, spatial, sonic, or conceptual correspondence the viewer can read at the splice. The outgoing frame and the incoming frame share a shape, motion, object class, or idea, so the cut argues a relationship instead of only changing the view.
p: In an early workshop scene, casually show a door that sticks unless lifted slightly. Later, during an urgent evacuation, a visitor fails to open it until the apprentice remembers the trick. Generate the same door hardware and motion in both scenes. Avoid a conspicuous explanatory close-up in the setup.

d: A match-motion cut continues direction and speed across the splice so the cut rides a vector even when location, time, or reality changes. One side of the join starts a movement; the other side keeps that movement, and the world around the body may be new.
p: Generate A: a woman falls backward onto a train berth. Generate B: the same woman completes the identical backward movement onto grass in a sunlit field. Match body pose, clothing, framing and velocity at the cut. Hard transition between worlds, no dissolving mattress or body morph.

d: A match split continues a graphic line or motion across a divide, so one contour belongs to two worlds at once. One side of the join is a pane or half-frame; the other is its partner; the shared edge, horizon, or gesture is the match.
p: Match split of [Subject], a graphic divide that continues a line or motion into another space.

d: Match on action cuts during one continuous action so the movement itself bridges two camera positions. The outgoing shot starts the gesture; the incoming shot finishes it, which is why the edit can change size or angle without feeling interrupted.
p: Generate A: wide view of a courier reaching for a door handle with the right hand. Generate B: close view from the same side of the action axis, continuing that exact reach and turning the handle. Cut during the reach, preserving hand, speed, sleeve and handle position.

d: Film montage creates meaning or compression through the ordered juxtaposition of shots. Each side of a join is a complete image; the claim lives in the order, the collision, or the months squeezed into a minute.
p: Create an essay montage alternating an automated sorting line with commuters moving through identical ticket gates. Match recurring barriers and mechanical rhythms to suggest institutional organization, while keeping humans visibly individual. No captions asserting the analogy as an objective fact.

d: Quick cuts editing strings shots shorter than a breath, so duration itself becomes rhythm, pressure, or music. Each side of a join is a full view from a changing setup; the meaning is the rate, not a skip inside one frame.
p: Create a tense three-person card-game ending. Begin with wide spatial views, then progressively shorter shots of faces, hands and one face-down card. Accelerate the cutting while preserving who sits where, then hold a long silent close-up before the card turns. Assemble rhythm in the edit.

d: A set transition lets the location change in camera: walls walk, architecture rewrites, one space becomes another without a hard cut. Both sides of the join are geographies that share a continuous camera path; the set itself is the editor.
p: The set around [Subject] transforms into a new location without a hard cut.

d: A smash cut makes an abrupt, high-contrast transition in image, sound, tone, scale, or time. The outgoing side has earned a state (quiet, prayer, resolution); the incoming side contradicts it without a polite blend.
p: After a conservator returns a stolen painting, show a calm closing sequence: gallery reopened, lights dimmed, doors locked. In one final locked shot, reveal a tiny fresh brushstroke appearing on the otherwise restored canvas. Keep the event subtle and consistent with earlier clues, not an unrelated shock.

d: Split screen shows two or more image fields at once, so separate spaces share a single moment on the same frame. Both sides of the join are visible together; there is no waiting for the next cut.
p: Show one lost-wallet incident three times: from the owner’s view, a cleaner’s view and a distant passenger’s view. Preserve the same station clock, movements and wallet position, but reveal different occluded actions each time. The third version resolves the apparent theft without inventing a new event.

d: Film transitions are designed joins: the splice treated as a visible gesture rather than as continuity glue. One side of the join and the other are planned as a pair, and the audience is meant to notice how we left A and entered B.
p: A designed transition around [Subject], the join as a gesture: wipe, morph, match, or light.

d: A wipe replaces one image with another through a moving boundary that travels across the frame. One side of the join is still A; the other side is already B; the edge between them is the edit, and it is meant to be seen.
p: Generate A: a traveler leaves a dusty village at dawn. Generate B: the traveler approaches a distant mountain pass later that day. Replace A with B using a clean left-to-right vertical wipe. Consistent travel direction, no blending or morphing scenery.

d: Atmospheric haze is scattering over distance: far planes go paler and often cooler, so kilometers of air become the depth cue. The particles are too small to read as drops; the air is matter you measure in ridges, not in globes around a near lamp.
p: Atmospheric haze stacking distance around [Subject], aerial perspective, far planes paler, depth as weather.

d: Dust motes are discrete particles hanging in a shaft of light, slow enough to read as time in still air. They are matter you can almost count; they live in the beam, not as a veil across the whole room.
p: Dust motes hanging in a shaft of light around [Subject], slow particles, a room that has been closed, time made visible.

d: Dust and sand as weather is mineral grit driven by wind until the sun is a dull coin and figures become silhouettes. The land attacks: particles occupy near air, sting highlights, and erase the horizon that haze would only pale.
p: Dust or sandstorm wrapping [Subject], sun as a dull coin, silhouettes, grit in the highlights, Sicario weather.

d: Fog is a dense local suspension of water droplets that collapses depth, turns lamps into globes, and delays the reveal of figures. The air is matter close to camera; geography hides until someone walks into the last few meters.
p: Dense fog around [Subject], depth collapsing, lamps becoming globes, figures appearing late, horror or London grammar.

d: Mist is a thinner water suspension than fog: pale layered air that still lets you read the next plane. Droplets are matter, but the veil is lyric, a morning or mountain breath rather than a wall.
p: Light mist around [Subject], softer than fog, morning or mountain breath, layers of pale air.

d: Ocean cinematography treats the sea as the other actor: swell, a horizon, salt light, a person against water that does not care. The atmosphere is spray, haze over distance, and a moving floor; the camera is in air, on a hull, or on rocks, not yet in the lung of the sea.
p: Ocean world of [Subject], swell, horizon, salt light, a person against water that does not care.

d: Rain in film is falling water that makes air visible as streaks and turns the ground into a mirror. Drops are matter in the optical path; without backlight they vanish, and without a wet-down the street stays dry under a fake storm.
p: Heavy cinematic rain around [Subject], backlit drops, wet-down pavement, umbrellas, silver streaks, weather as percussion.

d: Smoke is combustion particles with a source, a direction, and enough density to turn a room's air into a volume the light can strike. Unlike weather fog, it has a chimney, a cigarette, a tire, or a battlefield; backlight carves it into shafts and swirls.
p: Smoke around [Subject], cigarette, chimney, or battle, shafts of light catching it, volume in the room.

d: Snow is ice falling and settling: large flakes in backlight, a muffled world, tracks that record who passed. The air holds crystals you can size; the ground accumulates; contrast goes soft because the world has been covered.
p: Falling snow around [Subject], large flakes in backlight, muffled world, tracks, winter silence you can see.

d: Sparks and embers are incandescent particles thrown by welding, fire, grinding, or a cigarette: orange weather with short trajectories. They are burning matter; backlight is optional because they are their own small keys.
p: Sparks or embers around [Subject], welding, fire, cigarettes, orange particles as weather.

d: Steam is water vapor released where heat meets colder air: trains, manholes, showers, a white veil that rises and thins. It is wet matter, not combustion; it billows, condenses on lens and wool, and has a thermal source.
p: Steam billowing around [Subject], trains, manholes, showers, a white veil, industrial or intimate heat.

d: Underwater cinematography leaves air: the camera is in water, so caustics, buoyancy, and a missing horizon rewrite every edge. The medium is the matter; particles are silt and bubbles, and bodies move as if the world had gone slow without a slow-motion shutter.
p: Underwater of [Subject], caustics, muffled space, hair and cloth in slow water, a world without horizon.

d: A wet-down sprays pavement, asphalt, and cars so night lights double themselves in reflection, often with no rain in the air. The street is the effect; water is a surface treatment, not weather.
p: Wet-down streets around [Subject], pavement sprayed for night, double the lights by reflection, studio-night trick made beautiful.

d: Animation cinematography constructs light and motion instead of capturing them: graphic volume, designed keys, and movement as drawing, paint, or stepped CG, not as a photographed exposure. The world is built. Lens physics appear only if you choose them.
p: Animated cinematic treatment of [Subject], graphic volume, designed light, motion as drawing rather than photography.

d: Arthouse cinematography leaves space for thought: a static camera, odd headroom, natural or window light, and a frame willing to be empty. Duration is implied even in a still. The picture does not sell itself as a poster.
p: Arthouse still of [Subject], patience, odd headroom, natural light, the frame willing to be empty, duration implied.

d: Behind the scenes cinematography shows the making: C-stands, flags, the set wall, and crew in the same frame as the fiction, so the constructed world leaks. Documentary light (worklamps, mixed Kinos) sits beside the scene's key.
p: Behind-the-scenes look at [Subject], crew, stands, and the set edge visible, the fiction leaking, documentary light on a constructed world.

d: Blockbuster cinematography is high-contrast, billboard-readable coverage: clean skies or designed weather, a heroic rim on hair and shoulder, volumetric shafts, and a grade that often splits teal shadow from warm skin. The shot must still parse at poster size.
p: Blockbuster gloss on [Subject], expensive contrast, clean skies, heroic rim, IMAX-scale finish, adventure poster in motion.

d: Cinéma vérité uses available light, zoom-to-find framing, and the filmmaker's presence as a catalyst, so the camera is admitted into the room rather than hidden. Unpretty 16mm or digital frames, mixed color temperature, and a zoom hunting the moment are the physical signature, not a recovered amateur tape.
p: Cinéma vérité treatment of [Subject], available light, unpretty frames, zooming to find, life unstaged.

d: Cosmic horror cinematography builds dread from human insignificance: extreme long shots, slightly illegal geometry, under-light on faces, and a brightness that reveals too much. The threat is not a man. Scale, entity, and knowledge that will not fit a face are the optical problem.
p: Cosmic horror framing of [Subject], scale wrong, geometry slightly illegal, a brightness that reveals too much, human irrelevance.

d: Documentary cinematography mixes observational coverage with interview and archive rhetoric: unstyled wardrobe light, mixed color temperatures, a zoom finding focus, and respect without a glamour rim. Fictional films may borrow the same grammar as mockumentary. That is still documentary rhetoric, not a recovered camcorder tape.
p: Create a short mockumentary about a municipal committee preparing the world’s smallest parade. Intercut confident seated interviews with observational footage of tiny practical setbacks. Keep interview framing consistent, interviewer mostly offscreen and comedy grounded in sincere behavior rather than broad reaction faces.

d: The dreamcore aesthetic is a soft, liminal interior look: empty rooms, pools, and suburban halls lit by childhood practicals gone slightly wrong, with low contrast and unresolved space. Nostalgia is present. Safety is not.
p: Dreamcore image of [Subject], liminal rooms, soft dread, childhood lighting gone wrong, a memory that will not resolve.

d: Dystopian cinematography makes the civic system the antagonist: used architecture, haze, rank, and signage at a scale that already feels worn. The future is not shiny. It is bureaucratic, polluted, or monumental and cold, often in daylight as well as night.
p: Dystopian view of [Subject], civic scale gone cold, haze, signage, and rank, a future that already feels used.

d: Film noir lighting is a low-key, high-contrast setup: a hard key, often cut by a venetian gobo or a streetlamp cookie, leaves one cheek in true black while wet pavement returns silver. The camera sits at eye height on a 35mm or 50mm spherical lens, tungsten practicals as motivated sources, and blocking that isolates a figure in a doorway, an alley, or a pool of light.
p: Film-noir treatment of [Subject], hard venetian gobos, wet streets, fedora shadows, moral night, 1940s crime grammar.

d: The found footage look presents images as a recording made by someone inside the events, often later discovered or assembled, so the camera is a story object with a timestamp, a battery, and a reason to keep rolling. Consumer digital, Hi8, or MiniDV optics, autofocus hunt, and amateur framing are constraints, not decoration.
p: A volunteer records the final inventory of a closing observatory on a handheld camcorder. Every shot must have a plausible recording reason. When an unexplained door opens, the operator first documents the room number, then hesitates before following. Maintain limited battery, imperfect framing and consistent microphone perspective.

d: French New Wave cinematography shoots fiction on locations with street light, handheld 16mm or 35mm, and an edit that will jump-cut rather than cover. The frame jumps into walking life: cafes, sidewalks, apartments with mixed practicals, and a camera that admits it is a camera.
p: French New Wave energy on [Subject], jump cuts implied, street light, jump-into-life framing, handheld Paris oxygen.

d: German Expressionism cinematography treats the set as a mind: forced-perspective corridors, painted shadows, and jagged hard light replace natural architecture. The camera is often locked and slightly dutch, so the actor walks a geometry that already looks illegal.
p: German expressionist treatment of [Subject], painted shadows, impossible architecture, jagged light, Caligari psychology as set.

d: Giallo cinematography is Italian thriller grammar: hyper-saturated primaries from gelled windows and glass, fashion interiors, and a camera that often zooms rather than dollies toward threat. Beauty lighting sits on the victim. The violence is styled, not silver.
p: Giallo look on [Subject], hyper-saturated primaries, black leather gloves implied, Argento color crime, beauty as threat.

d: Magical realism cinematography treats an extraordinary event as ordinary inside a recognizable world: the same window light, the same 35mm coverage, with one impossible fact staged as if it were weather. The camera does not gawk, add a rim, or warp the lens.
p: Magical-realist image of [Subject], ordinary light, one impossible fact treated as weather.

d: Maximalist cinematography uses density as the point: too much color, too much pattern, ornament in every zone, and lighting that keeps the clutter readable rather than hiding it. Restraint would be a lie, so the frame is packed on purpose.
p: Maximalist frame of [Subject], too much color, too much pattern, density as the point.

d: Neo-noir cinematography keeps noir's hard keys and isolated blocking but replaces silver night with color: sodium vapor, neon practicals, and tungsten that stain rain and skin. The camera still hunts faces in shadow, yet the palette is contemporary, often cyan signage against warm flesh, not black-and-white contrast alone.
p: Neo-noir look on [Subject], color where classic noir was silver, neon practicals, rain, contemporary crime melancholy.

d: Photographic cinematography treats the movie as a print: a single decisive frame, posed or found light, often centered composition or tableau blocking, with the camera pretending it could hang on a wall. Motion is allowed, but the still is the law.
p: Still-photography grammar on [Subject], a single decisive frame, posed light, the movie pretending to be a print.

d: Pixel art builds the image from visible tiles or a low-resolution grid. The world is discrete squares, not continuous grain.
p: Pixel-art treatment of [Subject], chunky samples, limited palette, game-sprite cinema.

d: Southern gothic cinematography uses the American South as a humid optical problem: late-afternoon gold gone sickly, Spanish-moss dappled light, porch tungsten, and haze that keeps heat in the air. Decay is on the walls. The threat is family, history, and something under the porch, not a city streetlamp.
p: Southern gothic air around [Subject], humid decay, moss, late-afternoon gold gone sickly, beauty rotting.

d: Spaghetti western cinematography restages western iconography on Techniscope 2.35: dusty ochre landscapes, hard sun as the only key, and cuts from a 24mm plaza wide to a telephoto extreme close-up of eyes. Moral ambiguity sits in the hold on a face before anyone draws.
p: Spaghetti-western frame of [Subject], Techniscope grit, dusty ochre, extreme close-ups of eyes, sun as a weapon.

d: Stylistic suck is deliberate amateur cinematography: hunting zooms, cheap video, and the wrong white balance as a choice of the film's own camera, not necessarily of a character's recovered tape. Polish would be dishonest, so the image is ugly on purpose.
p: Deliberate amateur look on [Subject], bad zoom, cheap video, the wrong white balance as a choice.

d: Tech noir (also called future noir or cyber-noir) fuses noir's hard keys, rain, and guilty blocking with science-fiction production design: screens, LEDs, and corporate towers as practical sources. Analog crime grammar sits inside a digital city.
p: Tech-noir on [Subject], future crime, screens as practicals, rain, corporate night, analog noir in a digital city.

d: The vaporwave aesthetic is a pastel, low-contrast look: pink-cyan gradients, marble and palms, mall fluorescents, and VHS chroma bleed, as if a 1980s future never shipped. The camera is often centered and still. There is no crime geometry unless you add it.
p: Vaporwave treatment of [Subject], pink-cyan gradient, marble and palms, VHS bleed, mall-at-closing melancholy.

d: Video game cinematography uses playable camera logic: a follow cam, an isometric view, or an FPS eyeline, with space readable as a level and a HUD implied. Collision, boom height, and pathing constrain the lens the way a game engine would.
p: Video-game camera on [Subject], follow cam or isometric logic, HUD implied, space as a level.

d: The weirdcore aesthetic renders the familiar incorrectly: early-web compression, low-res sacred images, off-center crops, and a joke that is also a threat. The file looks like it should not have opened. Light is on-camera flash or a dim analog room, not a designed key.
p: Weirdcore image of [Subject], early-web dread, low-res sacred, a joke that is also a threat.

d: Wuxia cinematography stages martial chivalry in landscape: misted bamboo or desert silk, long-shot geography, and wire-assisted paths that read as weightless rather than as street punching. Color is costume and fog, not a gelled murder window.
p: Wuxia look on [Subject], misted bamboo, wire-fu weightlessness implied, silk color, heroic wides, Crouching Tiger air.

d: 2000s paparazzi, the 2000s paparazzi look, is on-camera flash from a compact digital: greenish white balance, hard wall-shadow, sidewalk glare, a face not ready. Fame as a strobe: the theft is the lighting.
p: 2000s paparazzi of [Subject], on-camera flash, compact digital, sidewalk fame, a decade of glare.

d: 3D render, the 3d render look, is a person as product visualization: clean global illumination, shader skin slightly too perfect, infinite cyc, contact shadows that never dirty. They should look computed, and photochemical grain is a joke if you add it.
p: A small fictional creature receives a repaired toy from a human friend. Preserve a specific performance: guarded gaze, delayed recognition, relaxed shoulders and a tentative reach. Stable character model, precise finger contact and matched eye level. Use performance reference and animation rather than relying on a generic happy expression.

d: Acid, the acid visual look, is a ruined print: burned chroma, melting edges, silver that shifted, dyes left in the sun too long. The dyes should misbehave, and a festive rainbow LUT is not damage.
p: Acid look on [Subject], burned chroma, melting edges, a print left in the sun too long.

d: Action figure, the action figure look, turns a person into merchandise: plastic joints, painted-on costume, blister-card studio lighting, a toy of a hero. Scale and material are the look, and a real actor in a costume is not enough.
p: Action-figure of [Subject], plastic joints, blister-card lighting, a toy of a person.

d: Agamemnon, the agamemnon look, is a named grade of hard sun, bronze bounce, and a dusk sky the color of a bruise, so a living body reads as antique metal. The name is not a shot: you still lock a height, pick a lens, and place a figure who can hold that weather.
p: Agamemnon look on [Subject], bronze, blood-dusk, tragic scale, a king under a bad sky, antique epic as grade.

d: Akrill, the acrylic paint look, is pigment as a plastic skin on the world: thick ridges, poster edges, high chroma, paint that still looks wet. Color sits on top: if it soaked in, you shot a wash.
p: Acrylic look on [Subject], thick plastic color, poster edges, paint that still looks wet.

d: Blue depth, the blue depth look, stacks cyan planes so distance is a blue gradient: underwater, night glass, or air thick enough that the far plane goes deeper than the near. Depth is a color, not a cool white-balance wash.
p: Blue-depth world of [Subject], stacked cyan planes, underwater or night glass, distance as a blue gradient.

d: Broken mirror, the broken mirror look, shards a person across cracked silver: one face that does not agree with itself, each shard a slightly different angle or time. Identity as a pile of cuts, and a crack overlay on a single face is not enough.
p: Broken-mirror of [Subject], silver shards, one face that does not agree with itself.

d: Canvas, the canvas painting look, is a photographic subject wearing oil: visible bristle, canvas tooth, thicker paint in the lights, eyes that still look. It is not a slider named oil: brushwork has direction and weight.
p: Canvas treatment of [Subject], visible brush, oil tooth, a painting that still has a face.

d: Casual monster slayer is deadpan heroism in ordinary clothes: supermarket wardrobe, impossible creature work, the same naturalistic light on both. The joke is register clash, and the camera should look like coverage of a commute, not a poster.
p: Casual monster-slayer of [Subject], everyday clothes, impossible creature work, deadpan heroism, a commute that includes a dragon.

d: Cold vision, the cold vision look, reads the world as temperature: either an arctic photochemical grade with breath and ice, or a thermal false-color overlay with heat edges. Empathy is not in the palette, so pick one sensor and keep it.
p: Cold vision of [Subject], arctic grade, thermal edges, a world seen as temperature and threat.

d: Comic, in comic book cinematography, inks a live-action frame: hard edges, halftone in the shadows, limited spots of color, a page that still has a photographed body in it. The camera still has a lens and one sun, and it is not a screenshot of a book.
p: Comic-book treatment of [Subject], inked edges, halftone, panel energy, a page that moves.

d: Dolphin ride, as a dolphin ride preset, is impossible tourism played straight: a body mounted on a sea creature, bright water, honest horizon, splash readable. The gag is the vehicle, and swimming near a dolphin is not the sentence.
p: [Subject] rides a dolphin through bright water, a tourist miracle.

d: Fairytale castle, the fairytale castle look, puts storybook stone and impossible turrets around a small figure, with dusk treated as illustration. Place first, person second: the name is a location law, not a camera move.
p: Fairytale-castle world around [Subject], storybook stone, impossible turrets, dusk as illustration.

d: Fallen angel, the fallen angel look, is holy light after the drop: a shaft of dirty church air, low-key flesh, wrecked wings implied by cloth, shadow, or light. The face is the altar, and costume is optional.
p: Fallen-angel image of [Subject], wrecked wings implied, church light, a holy fall, beauty after the drop.

d: Flash comic, the flash comic look, is comic ink plus a strobe bang: inked edges, halftone, and a hard white burst, print and paparazzi in one hit. A panel that detonates: quiet comic ink without the flash is the cousin, not this.
p: Flash-comic of [Subject], inked edges plus a strobe bang, print and paparazzi in one hit.

d: Hand paint, the hand paint look, is wet strokes laid over a living picture, a painter's wrist still in the shot or at least a stroke that just happened. Canvas is finished oil; this is paint as a verb.
p: Hand-paint over [Subject], wet strokes still moving, a painter

d: Ink riot, the ink riot effect, is liquid calligraphy occupying the air around a still-photographic subject: black and color blooming, dripping, exploding off a brush. The camera still needs a stand and a readable face, because the ink is weather, not a texture pack.
p: Ink riot around [Subject], black and color blooming in liquid, calligraphy as explosion, a page that fights.

d: Knight's diary, the medieval diary look, treats the frame as an illuminated page that still has mud on it: gold leaf as light, iron texture, dirt on cloth, a tired face like a saint who has been outside. It is period matter, not a plastic castle fair.
p: Knight

d: LSD, the lsd visual look, is an optical state: light trails, slight double edges, oversaturated practicals, walls on a slow inhale. Perception is the set, not a scene of drug use and not a rainbow LUT.
p: LSD look on [Subject], trails, breathing walls, too much chroma, a room that will not stay put.

d: Lava, in lava look cinematography, is molten light: black crust, orange wounds, heat as the key from below, air that shimmers. The ground is still deciding, and an orange grade on a normal street is not geology.
p: Lava light on [Subject], black crust, orange wounds, heat as the key from below.

d: Lost in a book, the lost in a book effect, uses an open volume as a door: near-plane paper, a gutter as threshold, illustration or weather coming out of the page, a reader looking in or falling in. A person reading on a couch is not the recipe.
p: Lost-in-a-book of [Subject], a reader falling into illustration, pages becoming rooms.

d: Magazine, in magazine cover cinematography, is a designed portrait with air for a masthead you will not render: fashion lighting, thumbnail-readable wardrobe, a page that knows it will be sold. Layout first, person second, and fake headlines will garble.
p: Magazine cover of [Subject], masthead space, fashion lighting, a page that knows it will be sold.

d: Marble, in marble look cinematography, is stone as flesh: veined whites, cold polish, a statue that still breathes. They should look quarried: pale beauty skin without veins is not mineral.
p: Marble look on [Subject], veined stone as flesh, cold polish, a statue that still breathes.

d: Mighty fighter, the mighty fighter look, is a living champion posed like cabinet art: oversized stance, hard rim, toy-box color, the city small behind them. It is a lock-off win pose, not a camera move and not motion blur.
p: Mighty-fighter frame of [Subject], toy-box combat, oversized stance, a champion posed for a cabinet art.

d: Modern, in modern architecture cinematography, makes the room the thesis: glass planes, a designed void, a person small in Mies-or-Ando geometry. Production design first, and a loft with string lights is not this.
p: Modern architecture around [Subject], glass planes, a designed void, the room as the thesis.

d: Monet muse, the monet look, dissolves a photographic scene into broken color: garden dabs, water as strokes, optical mix in the eye. Light is the subject, and defocus is not the same thing.
p: Monet-muse image of [Subject], broken color, garden light, water as dabs, impression as grade.

d: Multiverse, the multiverse look, puts the same person in parallel rooms, grades, and costumes at once, so one life is not the inventory. Versions must be separable: a double-exposure mush is not the recipe.
p: Plan three connected worlds: a real hospital room, a dreamed railway station and a deeper childhood kitchen. Give each one distinct sound, light and a recurring object. A falling cup in the hospital creates a distant rumble in the station and a tremor in the kitchen. Generate and edit the levels separately with a consistent causal map.

d: Noir, the noir preset look, is wet streets, venetian gobos, and a crime already in the lighting: a motivated hard key, black pools, a face half-deleted. Night is moral, and a dark photo with teal is not this.
p: Noir look on [Subject], wet streets, venetian gobos, a crime already in the lighting.

d: Orbital presence hangs a body in vacuum over a planet: hard unfiltered sun, no air fill, a sharp planetary limb, the person as a satellite. Put them in orbit: a studio globe behind an actor is not the recipe.
p: Orbital presence of [Subject], a body hanging over a planet, scale of prayer or threat, the person as a satellite.

d: Origami, in origami look cinematography, is paper as lawful sculpture: creases, planar color, a person or city becoming a fold. The world folds, and torn pulp without crease law is paper, not this.
p: Origami world of [Subject], lawful creases, planar color, a person or city becoming a fold.

d: Paper, in paper look cinematography, is the world as pulp: torn stock, visible fibers, a person as a cut-out on a page. The world is pulp, and creased lawful sculpture is origami, not this.
p: Paper world of [Subject], torn stock, visible fibers, a person as a cut-out on pulp.

d: Pearl earring, the pearl earring look, is a Dutch interior as grade: one north window, dark earth ground, skin like painted light, a small specular on a jewel. One window, one jewel, one look, and it is not a replica of a copyrighted painting.
p: Pearl-earring portrait of [Subject], Vermeer window, turban implied, a quiet Dutch interior as grade.

d: Penguin ride, as a penguin ride preset, is an absurd mount played straight: a person on a penguin through ice, slush, or the wrong city. The vehicle is the joke, and a penguin standing next to a person is not the sentence.
p: [Subject] rides a penguin through ice or city, a straight-faced gag.

d: Pigeons, as a pigeons video preset, is a city takeoff: a stable person and a flock bursting as confetti, wings filling the air, then settling. The flock is the move, and the person is the hold.
p: A flock explodes around [Subject], wings filling the air, then settling.

d: Puffin ride, as a puffin ride preset, is a commute on the wrong bird: a person mounted on a puffin against cliffs and spray, orange beak readable, played straight. A puffin next to a hiker is not the gag.
p: [Subject] rides a puffin against cliffs or surf, a straight-faced gag.

d: Race track, the race track look, pins a body or a machine to circuit geometry: oval, painted curbs, catch fencing, grandstands, speed as a closed loop. The oval is the set, and a car on a generic highway is not the recipe.
p: Race-track world of [Subject], oval geometry, painted curbs, grandstands, speed as a closed loop.

d: Random glow, the random glow look, is unmotivated orbs and analog leaks: a frame haunted by lamps that will not sit still. Optical accidents as style: even diffusion is the failure.
p: Random glow on [Subject], unmotivated orbs and analog leaks, a frame haunted by lamps.

d: Skatedog, as a skatedog preset, is pavement grammar: camera near the deck or the paws, wide lens, asphalt in the foreground, a creature or rider in street sport as a joke. Keep it stupid and low, because standing height is the failure.
p: Skatedog energy around [Subject], low wide, pavement, a creature or rider in street grammar, joke as sport.

d: Sketch, in sketch cinematography, is line on paper before paint: searching contours, hatching in the shadows, reserved paper in the lights, a drawing that still looks. Unfinished is the look, and a clean vector portrait is not.
p: Sketch treatment of [Subject], line, paper tooth, unfinished hatching, a drawing that still looks.

d: Superstar, the superstar look, is a face built for covers: beauty key, catchlights, a flash wall or crowd implied, wardrobe that photographs as money. Fame is a fact in the lighting, and the room is already looking.
p: Superstar treatment of [Subject], paparazzi bloom, flash wall, a face built for covers.

d: Toxic, in toxic look cinematography, is air as contamination: sick greens, yellow haze, fumes you can backlight. The air is a hazard, and a teal grade with no particles is not poison.
p: Toxic air around [Subject], sick greens, yellow haze, poison you can see.

d: Two color, in two color cinematography, is a duotone law: a pair of hues doing all the drawing, print as cinematography. Two inks, no extras: teal-and-orange with a thousand leftovers is not this.
p: A crowded monochrome railway platform, with only one small yellow suitcase retaining its natural color. Track the suitcase as it changes hands; all other objects stay black and white. Stable object identity, clean edge tracking, no random patches of color.

d: Ultraviolet, the ultraviolet lighting look, is black-light cinema: a UV lamp as author, whites that scream, colors that only exist under that tube. The unseen made loud: a purple LUT on daylight is not a black light.
p: Ultraviolet light on [Subject], black-light cinema, whites that scream, colors that only exist under that lamp.
